articles.title: At #MoveCebu forum, Cebuanos define what a liveable city should be
articles.summary: 'A liveable Cebu is one where no one is left behind,' says urban poor community leader Lourdes Bueza

items: Yumi Espina emphasized the need for a collective approach to address the liveability challenges in Metro Cebu, highlighting issues like waste management and flooding.
The forum gathered over 200 participants who discussed factors contributing to a liveable city, including stability, healthcare, culture, education, and infrastructure.
Community leaders stressed the importance of including marginalized groups in discussions about urban development and ensuring that no one is left behind in the pursuit of a liveable Cebu.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines – “If we want a liveable Cebu, we need to stop thinking as only a city but start thinking we are a Metro Cebu,” Yumi Espina, convenor of the Movement for Liveable Cebu said during the Sugbo Alang Sa Sugbuanon (Cebu for Cebuanos) public forum on Wednesday, October 14.

Espina shared his idea during the #MoveCebu roadshow at the University of San Carlos (USC) in Cebu City where more than 200 participants from civil society groups, youth-led initiatives, and academe gathered to get a better understanding of what makes liveable city.

Espina premised his statement amid the ongoing environmental and societal challenges Cebu has been facing, from waste management issues following the Binaliw landfill incident to struggles brought by heavy flooding in the metropolitan’s major urban and residential hubs.

“This forum was almost canceled because of the suspension of classes that was announced by the city mayor, ironically, because of poor air quality in so perhaps, it is one of the underlying causes why we must reflect on the issue of liveability,” Owen de La Victoria, OIC chair of the USC Department of Political Science, said in his welcome remarks.

In the days leading to the forum, the air quality in Metro Cebu dropped to very unhealthy levels due to localized emissions, made worse by unfavorable weather conditions, according to the Environmental Management Bureau in Central Visayas.

Espina listed the five major factors that make cities liveable: stability, healthcare, culture and environment, education, and infrastructure. Climate change and urbanization are the ultimate challenges to liveability, the architect said.

blocks.caption: UNDERSTANDING. Architect Yumi Espina of the Movement for Liveable Cebu breaks down the watershed system of Cebu and its links to the heavy flooding felt in the metropolitan areas. Photo by Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

blocks.text: “We experience flooding not just because rain is heavy but because urbanization has changed our waterways,” he added, citing the experience of La Paloma Village in Barangay Labangon in Cebu City which became a catch basin because of urbanization.

Espina presented the recommendations of the Cebu City Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP). The CLUP recommended the creation of a mass transit line, a “green belt” along the metropolitan’s major watersheds, and a “green loop” for the shift of urban development wherein urbanization moves eastward from the capital to Mactan Island.
The problem, Espina lamented, is that civil society groups are often left out in the discussions of developmental policies that the government and private sector typically have.

“What we need is a genuine partnership among government, business, and civil society, and an engaged citizenry that is willing to participate, speak up ,and hold institutions accountable,” Espina stressed.
As a reactor, Cebu City Councilor Joel Garganera conceded that the city government could have done so much more in promoting liveability with better planning and management.
“We are like in a dark room — blind and looking for a path out,” he said.
When asked how they would define liveable Cebu, speakers, reactors, and concerned citizens responded during the forum and on Muni in the Rappler app.

On the app, resident Asia Katrinah Atendido said that a liveable Cebu should be walkable, with walkable sidewalks that are not only used to park cars or any vehicles, serving the people and not vehicles
For University of the Philippines Cebu student Crispin Ginicez Caballero, a liveable Cebu would have continued improvement, expansion, and proper implementation of public transportation initiatives.

UP College of Communication, Art, and Design Dean Crina Tañongon emphasized the significance of empowerment in pushing for a liveable Cebu, adding that the academe must ensure that learners have the space to develop critical thinking.

blocks.caption: CONNECTING. ‘Students must ask why this is happening and that would lead to deeper understanding…it would be grounded on the shared realities that we face,’ UP College of Communication, Art, and Design Dean Crina Tañongon said.

blocks.text: Community leaders present during the forum pointed out how much of the lived realities of struggling Cebuanos showed a “grim picture” of the metro’s direction towards liveability.

Rebecca Herbese of Pangisda Cebu pointed out that small fisherfolks in Lapu-Lapu City struggled to find their own space amid campaigns for land reclamations and the presence of large fishing vessels within municipal waters.

“Mahimo lang liveable ang atong lugar karon kung ang atong mga katawhan dili na mag-antos sa kalisod (A place can only be considered liveable if the people no longer suffer from hardships),” Herbese said.

Joan Lucañas of urban poor rights group SILHIG said that Mandaue City residents feel left out in consultations for resettlement programs. She stressed the importance of creating a liveable city with the urban poor being seen as part of the population rather than a hindrance to the interests of developers.
United Fisherfolks and Urban Poor of Cebu City coordinator Lourdes Bueza asked: “Is empowerment just for the educated? Are the poor to be left out in that empowerment Cebu wants?”
“Ang liveable Cebu kay kanang wala mabiyaan (A liveable Cebu is one where no one is left behind),” Bueza said.
Rappler’s managing editor Miriam Grace Go shared the importance of putting community at the center of a city’s campaign for liveability.

“Cebu has had citizens who have been courageous enough to study the masterplans, to talk to residents, to engage with the residents…they all tell us the necessities of consultations, planning, and action,” Go said.
Go hoped that Cebu’s experts, journalists, and concerned citizens would share the discussions on liveability questions outside Cebu.

“Rappler is here to expand the awareness of its all-citizens-approach…to bring Cebu’s experience onto a larger stage so the other regions and communities will see that these are the same liveability challenges they are facing,” Go added.

The forum was organized by MovePH, Rappler’s civic engagement arm, in partnership with the University of San Carlos, the University of the Philippines Cebu; and Cebu Citizens Initiative and Movement for Liveable Cebu. It was supported by the government of Canada through its Canada Fund for Local Initiatives and by the Journalism for Nation Building Foundation.
Rappler officially launched the #PadayonCebu chat room on Rappler’s Muni at the public forum. Join the conversation on making Cebu liveable here. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Victoria to become first state to make abortions free as Coalition matches Labor election promise
articles.summary: Exclusive: Out-of-pocket costs for abortion care to be covered regardless of who wins November election as Jess Wilson says Liberals and Nationals ‘will not allow Labor to play…

blocks.text: Victoria will become the first state in Australia to make access to abortion care free, no matter who wins the November election, with the Coalition matching Labor’s promise just hours after it was announced as it attempts to neutralise the issue.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Thursday afternoon told Guardian Australia a Liberal National Coalition government would match Labor’s commitment to cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care up to 16 weeks’ gestation. This would include GP and specialist consultations, scans, tests or medication, which can quickly add up to more than $1,000.

The commitment means Victoria will become the first state in Australia to offer free universal access to abortion services, following the Australian Capital Territory which began covering out-of-pocket costs in 2023.

The Coalition would also expand the Victorian patient transport assistance scheme so that women in regional Victoria who must travel long distances for abortion care would also be eligible for subsidised travel and accommodation.
“The Liberals and Nationals will not allow Labor to play politics on this issue,” Wilson said.
“Labor has had 12 years to improve access to healthcare but are instead choosing to play politics.”

However, the Victorian opposition would not match Labor’s commitment to extend access to medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation or its plan to commission a clinical review into whether it could safely be offered at up to 12 weeks’ gestation.
Currently, medical abortion is subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for use up to nine weeks but the World Health Organization’s guidance allows for up to 12.
“Only Labor will protect a woman’s right to choose,” Labor’s health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said when she announced the election commitment on Thursday morning.

Stitt’s statement suggested that One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament. It read: “Polling shows the Liberals and One Nation can only form a government together. And One Nation wants to make abortion a criminal offence.”
However, Wilson on Thursday again ruled out changes to abortion laws under a Coalition government.
after newsletter promotion

“Victorians know where I stand on this issue. There will be no changes to abortion laws under a government I lead. Full stop. And I think it’s incredibly disappointing to see Labor playing politics with women’s reproductive rights five minutes before an election,” she said.
Wilson has previously described abortion as a personal decision that should be made by women in consultation with healthcare professionals.
The premier, Ben Carroll, earlier on Thursday said Labor “decriminalised abortion and we will stand up for it” as he warned that One Nation posed a threat.

“Let’s be very clear: you’ve seen the leader of One Nation very clearly say that he wants to roll back access to abortion. He wants to rob women of their right to choose their own future,” Carroll told reporters.
Abortion was decriminalised in Victoria in 2008, with women able to obtain a termination during the first 24 weeks of pregnancy, and later if they obtain the agreement of two doctors.

articles.title: Greens senator Jordan Steele-John takes leave amid investigation into complaints
articles.summary:
Steele-John said he rejected the claims and had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a ‘fair, independent process’

Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the…

blocks.text: Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the party room after complaints were made, triggering an independent review.
The Nine newspapers reported on Thursday afternoon that seven party members demanded an investigation into allegations he made inappropriate comments to a number of women.

Steele-John said he rejected the claims and had referred them to the Western Australian Greens for a “fair, independent process” that “upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved”.
“I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not,” he said in a statement.
“These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly. If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it.”
New Greens leader David Shoebridge said Steele-John had requested leave from the party room “and I have accepted it”.
Shoebridge said the party took “concerns of this nature extremely seriously”.
“This matter needs to be resolved via a fair and independent review that ensures all parties are entitled to natural justice and procedural fairness,” he said.
“The Australian Greens take complaints seriously, and as leader I want to make it clear that the integrity of the complaints process is essential.”
Guardian Australia has approached the Greens for further comment.

In his statement, Steele-John also said: “The letter says that victims of sexual and family violence should be at the centre of any investigation. I agree. In the one complaint of which I have been made aware, I am the person who experienced family violence.”

articles.title: Verse from the waste land: Rotterdam’s poetic bin lorries granted cultural status
articles.summary:
Lyrical lines printed on side of city’s fleet of rubbish trucks now recognised as one of Netherlands’ proud traditions

It is best known for its rich migration history and striking modern…

blocks.text: It is best known for its rich migration history and striking modern architecture. But now the Dutch city of Rotterdam is seeking recognition for a rather different characteristic: its tradition of printing poetry on bin trucks.

Since a poetry festival first came up with the idea in 1988, lines of verse have been printed on all of the city’s waste vehicles. The practice was this week elevated to the status of intangible cultural heritage, with formal recognition from a Dutch body that guards the nation’s traditions.

“Since 1988, poetry has been travelling through Rotterdam on our bin lorries,” said Joan Nunnely, the deputy mayor for culture, community and language. “You see it as you cycle to work or wait for a lorry to pass. Sometimes you read a line that stays with you for the rest of the day. What started as a quirky idea has become part of our city.”

blocks.caption: Rotterdam municipality celebrated the intangible heritage listing and unveiled its latest poetic lorries on Tuesday. Photograph: Rhalda Jansen Fotografie

blocks.text: The programme is democratising as well as uplifting, say its proponents. “Sometimes people think about culture as something only for those with a theoretical education,” said Nunnely. “This is one way to bring poetry to all Rotterdammers.”

For waste collection workers such as Paul Keijzer, who started driving Rotterdam litter trucks in 1988, the poetry gives an added connection to the city. He has even been inspired to write the odd line himself, he said, while the four trucks he has so far driven inspire all kinds of responses.
“We get positive reactions that people have never seen anything like it,” he said. “But sometimes they say: I don’t understand that line!” His truck currently bears a verse from Neeltje Maria Min:
Hoe langer ik terugkijk hoe Strakker de knoop in de tijd.
Or: The longer I look back the Tighter the knot in time.

blocks.caption: A poem by Roland Jooris, on the side of a Roteb garbage truck as part of the Poetry International project in 1988, reads: ‘Thanks, just some applause is enough’. Photograph: Rotterdam Stadsarchief

blocks.text: Diana Chin-A-Fat, director of Poetry International, which came up with the initiative, said they and Rotterdam municipality had approached the heritage body with a plan to preserve this tradition. “It’s become so much a part of the city,” she said. “Every Rotterdammer recognises it. Every Rotterdammer reads it. It’s unique.”

Poet and spoken word artist Derek Otte said it also demonstrated how Rotterdam was carving out a modern identity. “You can switch Amsterdam for Leiden or Delft and they are all beautiful – but Rotterdam is something else,” he said. “That initial idea was to combine something beautiful like poetry with something beautiful in a different way, like the garbage trucks. It’s a way to say the important things in life, in as few words as possible.”
His own words have recently joined the fleet. In Dutch, they read:
Van stenen gaat een stad de hoogte in De mensen geven diepte.
Or: Stones build a city high. The people give it depth.

In its inventory of more than 400 traditions, crafts, rituals and customs, the Dutch Centre for Intangible Cultural Heritage aims to document the Netherlands’ unique cultural characteristics. These range from the annual Pride Amsterdam festival and its parade of colourful boats along the capital’s canals to the 10 remaining shepherded flocks of sheep.
Several Dutch traditions are recognised in Unesco’s international list, such as traditional irrigation and the craft of the miller operating windmills and watermills.

articles.title: Mother of drug victim killed over mistaken identity clings to hope for justice
articles.summary: 'Hindi ko naman iniisip na mapapatay ‘yong anak ko na wala namang kinalaman sa mga sitwasyon na iniisip nila…. Ang dami kong ‘bakit’ na tanong na walang sagot,' says Lorna Pepaño

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – “Kahit justice delayed, justice denied, umaasa pa rin kami (Even if it’s justice delayed, justice denied, we’re still holding on to hope),” said single mother Lorna Pepaño whose son, Christian, was a victim of extrajudicial killing in 2020.
Pepaño, 72, recounted the killing of her son during the fourth truth-telling session of the Philippine Truth Commission on October 9.
Christian, 39, was shot four times by riding-in-tandem gunmen in Quezon City on the early evening of May 18, 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic.
According to Pepaño, Christian headed outside to buy her maintenance medicine for hypertension. An hour later, a neighbor told her that her son was shot dead just blocks away from their house.
The perpetrators allegedly mistook her son for their supposed victim because they were wearing the same clothes.

“Ginaya [ng mga hinahabol ng ‘riding-in-tandem’] ‘yong damit ng anak ko, kaya ‘yong anak ko ang na-target (My son was targeted because the person the riding-in-tandem was pursuing wore the same clothes),” said Pepaño.
The perpetrators initially fired four shots at Christian, but the latter still managed to run away. Unfortunately, they caught up with him in the streets of Barangay Holy Spirit, where he was killed.
“Hindi po ako ‘yon…. Hindi po ako ‘yon (It’s not me…. it’s not me),” were Christian’s last words before he was mistakenly shot death, Lorna recounted.
“Pare, hindi siya ‘yong target natin. Mali (He’s not our target. We got it wrong),” Pepaño recalled the perpetrators’ belated realization.
She added: “Bakit? Nagbase ba sila sa damit? Kaya isinisigaw ko na hindi ganoon ‘yong anak ko. Porke’t ganoon ‘yong damit niya, suspect na?”
(Why? Did they just base it on clothes? That’s why I’m insisting that my son is not who they claim to be. Just because of his clothes, he’s already a suspect?)
The day Christian was killed, Pepaño said she saw the perpetrators and their supposed target loitering outside their residential compound.

“Sumisilip sa compound namin pero ‘di ko pinapansin kasi wala naman akong pakialam sa kanila kung ano man sila. Hindi ko naman iniisip na mapapatay ‘yong anak ko na wala namang kinalaman sa mga sitwasyon na iniisip nila. Masakit…. Ang dami kong ‘bakit’ na tanong na walang sagot,” Pepaño added.

(They were peeking in our compound, but I ignored them because I didn’t care whoever they were)I never thought my son would get killed over the situations that they accuse him of. It hurts… I have so many why’s that were never answered.)

blocks.caption: NOT FORGOTTEN. An empty chair memorial for Christian Pepaño. A good son to his mother and brother to his siblings, Christian was supposed to buy his mother’s hypertension maintenance medicine before he was gunned down in Quezon City on May 18, 2020. Rhen Peñada/Rappler

blocks.text: Christian’s killers have yet to be tracked down.

Established on May 27 this year, the Philippine Truth Commission is an independent, civilian-led institution that documents violations and extrajudicial killings connected to the war on drugs campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte. The commission brings together testimony, records, research, and public truth-telling sessions for policy advocacy and institutional reforms.
Duterte, who faces three counts of crimes against humanity, is currently detained in the International Criminal Court at The Hague, Netherlands, after his arrest in March 2025.

Forensic pathologist and truth commissioner Dr. Raquel Fortun said she was skeptical about the issued death certificate to Christian’s family. Like other drug war victims, Fortun and her team also conducted n examination of Christian’s remains.

Signed May 20, 2020, or two days after Christian’s death, the death certificate claimed that the victim had only around two minutes to live after receiving the fatal gunshot wounds to his head and trunk.

“‘Pag tiningnan ‘nyo ‘yong injuries niya, I doubt tumagal siya ng isang minuto sa grabe nang tama niya (If you take his injuries into account, I doubt he even lasted a minute due to the gravity of the shots he sustained),” Fortun argued.

Not only that, Fortun was also surprised by the doctor’s decision to put “homicide” as the victim’s manner of death. She explained that even doctors do not usually put “homicide” in cases involving gunned-down victims.
Despite the lack of police reports and forensic evidence, Fortun was able to confirm that Christian died of multiple gunshot wounds to the head and trunk.

“Pinagyayabang ng PNP (Philippine National Police) na meron silang IDs, raid lists, and then hitlists…. May laman ba ‘yong database nila (The PNP boasts they have IDs, raid lists, and then hitlists…. Does their database contain anything)?” Fortun questioned the PNP’s lack of evidence in the said incident.
“Kaya tuloy-tuloy ang patayan kasi walang imbestigasyon (Killings persist because there are no investigations),” Fortun added.

blocks.caption: FINDINGS. Forensic pathologist and truth commissioner Dr. Raquel Fortun presents her team’s findings on the remains of the late Christian Pepaño during the truth-telling session. Rhen Peñada/Rappler

blocks.text: The Philippine Truth Commission is set to have its first conference on November 23, to release its first report on its independent investigations and documentation of Duterte-time killings. – Rappler.com

Rhen Peñada, a Rappler intern, is a junior information technology student from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines-Santa Rosa, Laguna campus. He is a former staffer of his school paper, “Ang Alpas.”

articles.title: Lacson: Remaining P11-M budget for impeachment trial more than enough
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson, chairman of the Senate Committee on Accounts, said Thursday that the upper chamber still has P11 million remaining in the allocated budget for the conduct of the…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 11:38am

Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson, chairman of the Senate Committee on Accounts, said Thursday that the upper chamber still has P11 million remaining in the allocated budget for the conduct of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte—an amount that is enough to cover the rest of the proceedings.

Lacson said the P11 million came from the P25.7-million continuing appropriation under the 2025 General Appropriations Act (GAA). The original appropriations for the trial amounted to P27.5 million, but roughly P2 million was already spent previously for the robes of the senator-judges and other items.
Of the P25.7-million, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said that P14.55 million, or about P330,763 per day, was spent over the past 44 trial days, including whole day trials.
"Ang huling kwenta ni Senate President, nasa mga P14 million plus pa lang ang nagagastos out of the P25 million na inabot namin," Lacson said in an interview on Super Radyo dzBB.
(According to the Senate President's latest computation, only a little over P14 million has been used out of the P25 million allocation that remains.)

"Sapat na 'yung P25 [million] na naiwan dahil kung P14 million, mayroon pang mga P11 [million]... Kakasya na 'yun kasi isang article na lang ang naiwan at saka presentation na ng defense so hindi na magtatagal 'yun. Sosobra pa 'yun actually, may mase-save pa du'n," he continued.

(The P25 million that remains is sufficient—since only P14 million has been used, there is still about P11 million left... That will be enough, as the defense will already present, so the trial won't take much longer. In fact, we would still be able to save some funds.)
Both Gatchalian and Lacson have denied that the Senate was spending P25 million daily for the impeachment trial of Duterte.

Their statements were issued after Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., spokesperson for the vice president, claimed that approximately P500 million—or P25 million per day—has been used by the Senate over a span of 20 trial days for Articles I and IV.
Considering other expenses, and the "wasted salaries" of members of Congress who participated in the trial, Panelo said the public cost for hearing the dropped articles would exceed P1 billion.

Gatchalian said the P14.55 million expenses of the Senate for the trial so far covered meals for personnel during extended sessions, supplies, overtime pay, and the rental of a venue outside the chamber's premises for the conduct of budget deliberations, as the trial occupied most of the Senate's available rooms.
"The Constitution gives the Senate the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment. The Senate is fulfilling this duty as required by law," he said.
"We extended our hours and devoted full days to the trial so it could proceed at an acceptable pace, without unduly disrupting the Senate's legislative work and daily operations," he added.

During the trial on Tuesday, the prosecution manifested that they would no longer pursue Articles I, III and IV against the vice president, regarding allegations on the misuse of confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats, respectively.

With the decision, the prosecution would only push for Article II, which concerns allegations that Duterte failed to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.
The Senate impeachment court has accepted the move by the prosecution to withdraw three of the four impeachment articles. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Anthropic flags revenue surge to investors ahead of stock market debut
articles.summary: It comes as some investors have become concerned about the amount of money being spent on AI infrastructure.

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

The figures were revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.

It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have come under pressure over concerns about the large amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.
Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.

In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by more than 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 9.4% and SK Hynix dropping 10.8%.
Tech-heavy indexes in the region were also down. South Korea's Kospi was 7.6% lower while Japan's Nikkei 225 fell by 4.8%.

articles.title: Brazil to shorten workweek in win for Lula ahead of runoff
articles.summary: Brazil's Senate approved cutting the workweek from 44 to 40 hours. The move could give President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva an edge over his opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, ahead of the October 25 runoff.

image.caption: Amendment lowers working hours from 44 hours a week to 40, providing Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a key legislative win ahead of Oct. 25 runoff [Photo: October 11]Image: Paulo Lopes/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Brazil's Senate on Thursday approved a constitutional amendment to reduce the working week to five days from six without a salary cut, likely providing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with an edge ahead of Flavio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff on October 25.
Lula is expected to sign the shorter workweek into law next week.

Brazil's leftist leader has taken a number of steps in recent days to shore up support before the runoff, including new fuel tax cuts, extending existing subsidies and pledging to pardon the debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses to the federal government and others.
But the pledge to trim the workweek turned into a top promise that Lula hoped to deliver on before the runoff.
Brazil election: Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro in runoff
"6x1" reform receives overwhelming support
The new amendment, known as the "6x1" reform, could benefit more than 37 million workers, according to the government.
"The end of the 6x1 is more than a change in the workday. It's more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow, take care of yourself, and enjoy life," Lula wrote on X.
"Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve time to live. It's a victory for workers. It's Brazil ready for more," he said.
But the legislation still leaves out a large number of people in the shadow economy, like freelancers and delivery drivers.
Lula, a former trade unionist, worked on the proposal to reduce the workweek with his government over the course of the year.
Bolsonaro backs "6x1" reform after opposing it

Flavio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator and the eldest son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, had long opposed the legislation. But Flavio Bolsonaro reversed course on Tuesday to say that he'll back the bill because it has so much support.

Many businesses opposed the bill because it would raise their costs, and Bolsonaro previously argued for estabilishing a flexible payment regime where individuals negotiate their pay with their employers.
He repeatedly called the legislation election-motivated.
In the first round of elections earlier this month, Bolsonaro dealt Lula a bruising defeat, finishing ahead with 47% of the vote, though short of the 50% needed for an outright majority.
The campaign in Brazil has been dominated by voter frustration over high street crime, the strength of Evangelical churches, the high tax burden for businesses and economic dissatisfaction.

articles.title: El Niño damage to agriculture hits P6.8 billion
articles.summary: Agricultural damage has reached P6.8 billion this year as several areas struggle with dry spells linked to the very strong El Niño phenomenon in recent months.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 11:13am
Farm workers check on their crops, spray organic pesticides, and remove unwanted weeds at a rice field in Tanay, Rizal on Sept. 19, 2023.
Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — Agricultural damage has reached P6.8 billion this year as several areas struggle with dry spells linked to the very strong El Niño phenomenon in recent months, according to the Office of Civil Defense (OCD).

OCD spokesperson Junie Castillo said on Thursday, October 15, that while the amount accounts for the total damage recorded this year, the reduced water supply for irrigation due to lower rainfall has negatively affected crop production in some areas over the past two months.

“May mga nakaranas na nung dry spells at drought. Ibig sabihin, mga two months na bawas na sa mga pag-ulan, kaya ‘yung mga patubig sa mga agrikultura, kaya nagkaroon na rin ng kabawasan sa produksyon ng iba’t ibang crops sa iba’t ibang lugar,” Castillo said in an interview with dzMM.

(Some areas have already experienced dry spells and drought. That means rainfall has been reduced for the past two months, and so has irrigation for agriculture, resulting in a decline in the production of different crops across different areas.)

The agency added that, as of press time, 109 areas had already declared a state of calamity due to the impacts of El Niño, with most local government units expressing concerns over agricultural damage.
Concerns on rice, vegetable supplies

The Philippine Chamber of Agriculture and Food Inc., a private-sector group focused on agribusiness and food security, has also expressed concerns about the impacts of El Niño on the agriculture sector, including vegetable and rice supplies.

The group’s president, Danilo Fausto, said on Thursday, October 15, in a separate interview with dzRH that the rice supply of the National Food Authority (NFA) is currently insufficient and may last only 51 days, instead of the ideal 70 to 90 days.

He also warned that several factors, including the depreciation of the peso, rising importation costs, and the impact of El Niño on other countries from which the Philippines usually imports rice, may drive up domestic rice prices.

Fausto also said that while vegetable production is currently in favorable condition and is expected to remain so until the end of 2026, harvests may decline by the first quarter of next year as dry conditions worsen.

“We are expecting this last quarter meron tayong mga gulay…kasi maganda ang harvest natin. Ang problema pagdating mo next year ng first quarter towards March tuyot na ‘yan so hindi masyadong lalaki ang mga gulay,” Fausto said.

(We are expecting this last quarter that we will have vegetables… because our harvests are good. The problem is when drought comes in the first quarter towards March next year, the vegetables may no longer grow properly.)
Gov’t interventions

The OCD said the government has provided about P10 billion worth of assistance, particularly through the Department of Agriculture (DA), to help farmers prepare for the anticipated worsening dry conditions.
According to Castillo, the assistance included the distribution of water pumps, seeds and fertilizers, as well as livelihood support programs.

He also mentioned that the government has a National Action Plan for El Niño to monitor and address the situation in the areas of food security, water security, health security, energy and public safety during the phenomenon.

The state weather bureau PAGASA had earlier reported that drought may affect all provinces in the country in March 2027, warning the public of potential El Niño risks such as water shortages and heat-related illnesses.

articles.title: Texas Democrat James Talarico faces grilling from voters at town hall in tight Senate race
articles.summary:
Talarico casts himself as a moderate who would put Texans’ needs over party allegiances amid close contest against Republican Ken Paxton

James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for…

blocks.text: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with several undecided voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall on Wednesday evening.
One voter, a devout small business owner, questioned the authenticity of Talarico’s faith, referencing a past remark where he described God as nonbinary.

“When I said that, I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico responded. “What I was saying is actually not controversial theologically: the idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that – the late Pope Benedict said that.”
Talarico added that he was receptive to feedback from Christians.

Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?”
Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”.

“We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies.
During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy.

Talarico and the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, are locked in a competitive race to become Texas’s next US senator, with most recent polls showing Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton. (Paxton declined an invitation to appear on CNN, host Erin Burnett said at the start of the town hall.)

Though Democrats have not won a Senate seat in the state since the late 1980s, they’re hoping Talarico’s newcomer energy and popular appeal will persuade independents and Republicans fed up with Donald Trump’s second term – or turned off by Paxton’s many scandals.

Over the weekend, Talarico became the subject of a disinformation campaign after he was absent from the campaign trail for more than a week. While Talarico’s campaign repeatedly said the candidate was sick with a bad case of the flu, conservative influencers falsely accused him of receiving medical treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.
The rumor was further propelled by Paxton and Trump, who sought to fuel skepticism about Talarico’s health and fitness for office.
The Democratic candidate denied the false allegations after returning to the campaign trail last week, noting he had never been to Ohio.

“False claims got millions of views online and this is an example of what I call the ‘rage economy’,” Talarico said during the town hall. “Billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table, put gas in the tank, or improve our communities.”

Paxton, meanwhile, has been battling his own controversies. A series of leaked audio recordings – made during a closed-door meeting – have been posted online and revealed him being critical of his own party and campaign leaders in DC.

Paxton entered the race with a history of scandals. He was impeached by the Texas state legislature in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust, though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife of almost four decades, Angela Paxton, then filed for divorce in 2025 on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery.
But Trump endorsed Paxton to run against Talarico, passing up incumbent Republican John Cornyn.

articles.title: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived.

blocks.text: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."

She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.

Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.

In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

items: A group of 40 state attorneys general is urging a US bankruptcy judge to ensure the protection of young users' data during Character.AI's bankruptcy proceedings.

A group of 40 state attorneys general on Wednesday, October 14, urged a US bankruptcy judge in Delaware to protect young users of Character.AI and keep their data safe during the AI companion company’s bankruptcy.

Character.AI filed for bankruptcy late on Monday and is seeking to use its Chapter 11 case to resolve the states’ investigations and lawsuits, license its technology to Disney for $20 million, and seek a buyer willing to take on its chatbot business.

Abigail Ryan, an attorney for the states, told US Bankruptcy Judge Brendan Shannon in Wilmington that the states are negotiating a settlement with Character.AI over allegations its chatbots impersonated licensed medical professionals and exposed children to sexualized and abusive interactions.
Even so, Ryan said, the states want to make sure that any buyer of Character.AI’s assets will protect users’ chat histories and improve safety features.

“We’re willing to work with the buyers to find safeguards, but we don’t want to see what has transpired in the past start over with a new purchaser,” Ryan said at the company’s first hearing in US bankruptcy court.

“This company has collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, said in a Wednesday statement issued just before the court hearing.
Character.AI’s attorney, Erin Fay, said she heard those concerns “loud and clear,” but said that no buyer has yet made an offer for the company’s user data or its operating chatbot business.

The company’s platform allows users to interact with and create generative AI characters customized by user prompts and often modeled on fictional characters, celebrities, and historical figures. Its active users spend an average of two hours a day talking to the chatbots.

Beyond the states’ claims, Character.AI has been sued by families who allege that its chatbots gave harmful advice, contributed to the suicides of two children, and exposed children to sexualized and bullying interactions. Character.AI has reached preliminary settlements with five of those families.
The company also faces investigations by the US government and by authorities in the UK, Italy, Russia and Australia.

Disney has agreed to pay $20 million to license the company’s technology and intellectual property, as well as hiring most of Character.AI’s staff, but is not interested in the type of data that the state AGs are worried about, Fay said. Disney’s asset purchase must be approved by the bankruptcy court, and it is subject to higher offers.
Fay described a grim mood within the company in recent months, saying that employees “were very excited about the product and the user base” but had “lost faith in the company’s trajectory.”

The company attributed its bankruptcy to legal expenses and the high price for computing power and AI talent, saying it was losing between $8 million and $9 million a month before filing for Chapter 11 protection.

Character.AI’s management became concerned about its ability to survive employee attrition by late summer. In September, Disney stepped in to hire most of the company’s employees and allow them to work on keeping Character.AI afloat during a bankruptcy sale process and technology transition, according to court filings. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff
articles.summary:
Congress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could effect up to 30 million

Brazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working week to a maximum of 40 hours, a move that could affect 30 million workers and that will hand a political victory to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the presidential runoff in under two weeks.

In an attempt to overturn the first-round lead secured by his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula has strongly championed the amendment, which will give some workers an extra day off each week.

Bolsonaro, by contrast, spent months opposing the change but reversed course on Tuesday, saying “the majority of Brazilian workers” supported it. On Wednesday, he joined 75 senators who approved the reform, which passed the lower house in May.
Only one senator voted against it: Hamilton Mourão, former vice-president to Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father.
The constitutional amendment bans six-day workweeks, currently worked by 16 million people, while cutting the maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours for more than 30 million workers.

The change is expected to affect mainly workers in retail, restaurants and hotels, most of them low-paid – one of the groups which Lula lost the most support from since the 2022 election, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Lula celebrated the amendment’s passing, writing on social media “ending the 6x1 schedule is about more than changing working hours. It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life.”
Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, said the change “could indeed benefit Lula’s re-election campaign”.
The proposal began as a TikTok movement called Life Beyond Work, founded by a pharmacy assistant who entered politics after its success and later was embraced by Lula.

His party spent months pushing the senate to put the proposal to a vote and many believed that after the far right’s sweeping victory last week secured a broad congressional majority in 2027, the Senate would no longer vote on it.
But Senate president Davi Alcolumbre, whose relationship with Lula has at times been rocky, put it to a vote.
Flávio Bolsonaro’s party had considered blocking it, but polls showed the change had more than 70% of the general population behind it, and more than half of the senator’s voters.
In May, Bolsonaro said the proposal could cause “mass unemployment”, an argument employers’ associations opposed to the change have repeatedly made.
The senator voted remotely while campaigning in the country’s south.

Even after changing his position, Bolsonaro said on Tuesday that he “supports something even better,” referring to an alternative proposal he had long advocated in which pay would be based on the hours actually worked. The Folha newspaper reported that he told business leaders that, if elected, he would review parts of the new amendment, a point several allied senators also made during Wednesday’s vote.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s right-wing Senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro delivers a speech on Wednesday.  Photograph: Sílvio Ávila/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite its approval, none of the changes will take effect before the runoff on 25 October. After the Senate president promulgates it, a 60-day period will follow before six-day workweeks are abolished and the maximum working week is reduced from 44 to 42 hours, then to 40 hours after a further 14 months.

However, Escobar believes its approval could already benefit Lula: “It will speak to how voters feel economically when they cast their ballot; they can feel more relieved with a change in their working schedule”.

Marilane Oliveira Teixeira, a professor and researcher at a study centre at the University of Campinas who has spent months examining the possible impacts of the change, said there was no shortage of evidence showing how harmful having only one day off is to workers.

“People who work a 6x1 schedule are practically prevented from having even a minimum level of social life,” she said, adding that the negative effects could include illness, workplace risks and exhaustion, “especially for women, who still carry the burden of unpaid domestic work”.

Lilian Cristo dos Santos, 50, has only one day off from her job as a saleswoman at a home appliances shop in Salvador, Bahia. “There’s no time to go to the doctor, to the beach, to the salon, to look after myself; I wanted to have time to study and I can’t. On my only day off, I have to clean the house and look after my family,” she said.
Santos said she voted for Lula, but has colleagues who chose Bolsonaro. “They say he represents change – well, yes, but certainly for the worse.”

Escobar is among many political scientists who believe that, despite Bolsonaro’s lead, Lula has gained momentum not only from the change to the working schedule, but also from demonstrations by his supporters that have drawn thousands across the country and an effort to build a stronger presence on social media.

Lula also continued announcing benefits just days before the vote, including debt relief for microentrepreneurs, and published a letter to evangelical Christians – who have historically favoured Bolsonaro – stressing his commitment “to ensuring that everyone has two days off a week, because life is not just about work”.

Escobar said: “Although most people have already decided their vote, there are some who are more responsive to political moves, and Lula has been trying very strongly to reach them. … The race still looks somewhat tangled, tied, with some degree of advantage for Bolsonaro, but it is still a very open election.”

articles.title: Senior Victorian public servants hid loss of up to $285m from Covid grants given to ineligible businesses
articles.summary:
Whistleblowers applauded as Ibac finds ‘decisions were made to withhold information about the magnitude of the loss’

Senior public servants in one state covered up losses suspected to be…

blocks.text: Senior public servants in one state covered up losses suspected to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars arising from flawed Covid-19 business support payments, an investigation has found.
During the pandemic, the Victorian government spent an estimated $257m on support grants to 9,000 ineligible businesses.
An investigation by the integrity watchdog has found senior officials within the department responsible for making those payments covered up the extent of the losses from their managers.
“This was not a one-off event, nor was it due to an oversight,” the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission report reads.
“Decisions were made to withhold information about the magnitude of the loss and misleading information was subsequently created and disseminated over an extended period of time.”
Tabled in parliament on Thursday, the Operation Harmonia special report probed conduct by officers within the since-replaced Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions.

items: Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

blocks.text: It concerned their response to revelations the department had granted millions in support payments to ineligible businesses during the early days of the pandemic.
By mid-2021, then-premier Daniel Andrews’ government department, was aware of potential issues relating to its use of GST as a metric, the investigation found.

When the true scale of the losses came into view, suspected to be as high as $285m, the associate secretary and deputy secretary opted to withhold that information from their superiors, the report said.

The deputy secretary directed that all information about the suspected losses be wiped from a draft report to the then-minister for Industry Support and Recovery Martin Pakula and the Victorian Auditor General’s Office, the report said.

Ibac found that in 2022, after the auditor general opened an audit of the grants, the deputy secretary prepared a brief to then-minister Ben Carroll, which contained “false and misleading” information.

That brief claimed Carroll’s predecessor, Pakula, had been aware of and approved the department’s approach to assessing grants and that no payments had been made in error, but Ibac found “the assertion that Minister Pakula was ‘fully apprised of and approved the department’s implementation approach’ was disingenuous”.
The watchdog made no adverse findings against Carroll, who now serves as Victorian premier.
Ibac commissioner, Victoria Elliott, said the conduct exposed by the investigation fell short of the expectations of senior public officers.

“This special report exposes serious failures by senior public officers, and informing Victorians of these findings is crucial in promoting transparency and accountability in the public sector,” she said.
The investigation was triggered after whistleblowers brought allegations of corrupt conduct within the department, which was replaced by the Department of Jobs, Skills, Industry and Regions in 2023.
“I want to applaud the whistleblowers who came forward to Ibac in Operation Harmonia,” Elliot said.
“Your bravery is critical in ensuring this conduct is not only exposed but that Victoria’s public sector can take these findings and apply the learnings to their own organisations.”

articles.title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel 'barbaric' execution livestream
articles.summary: Livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," 72 former officers said in a letter.

blocks.text: A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

"We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr".
Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base.
Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan.

Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported thatTrump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday.

In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out.

But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators".
"This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote.

"It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers."
The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars.

Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.

Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter.
So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head of Nasa, and a retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army.

articles.title: [Good Business] Rethinking enterprise as a force for good
articles.summary: The challenge is not simply to declare that business should be a force for good. It is to make that commitment visible in how capital is invested, people are treated, and growth is pursued.

blocks.text: What does it mean for a business to do good? Is it enough to create jobs, donate to communities, or support social causes? Or should we examine something more fundamental: how a business earns, whom it serves, and what its success makes possible for others?

These questions were at the heart of the Business as a Force for Good (BFG) Summit 2026, held on October 9 at Makati Shangri-La. The discussions challenged a familiar assumption that profitability and social impact belong to separate agendas. More importantly, they invited business leaders to consider whether their purpose is reflected not only in their stated values, but also in their everyday decisions.

One idea offered by Ramon R. del Rosario Jr. provides a useful starting point: identify an unmet societal need, then build a sustainable business to address it. This two-step approach presents social challenges not simply as problems for philanthropy to solve, but as opportunities for enterprises to create lasting value. Yet recognizing a need is only the beginning. The harder task is building a business that can respond to it effectively, responsibly, and over time.

This distinction matters because good intentions alone cannot sustain meaningful impact. An enterprise may have a compelling mission, but without sound financial management and operational discipline, its ability to serve people remains fragile. Conversely, a profitable business may still fall short of being a force for good if its growth does little to address the needs of the communities around it. Purpose and performance must therefore reinforce one another.

The summit’s conversations about impact investing brought this challenge into sharper focus. If underserved communities represent significant unmet needs, why does so little capital reach enterprises working to address them? Expanding shared prosperity requires more than individual companies with admirable missions. It also calls for an ecosystem in which investors, businesses, civil society, and government can work together to direct resources toward meaningful and sustainable outcomes. Trust and collaboration are not peripheral concerns; they help determine which ideas receive the opportunity to grow.
But even a well-funded enterprise must ask a deeper question: what kind of progress are we pursuing, and for whom?

The discussion on Pamamahalang Pilipino offered a distinctly Filipino perspective through concepts such as kapwa, the recognition of shared personhood, and loob, the inner values that shape our choices. (READ: [Good Business] Kaloob and kapwa: Agrabah Ventures on co-creating a bountiful tomorrow)

These ideas challenge organizations to look beyond employees as units of productivity or communities as markets to be served. They encourage leaders to recognize the people behind business outcomes and consider whether their decisions contribute to a more dignified and humane life.

This perspective also changes how success is understood. Growth can be measured in revenue, expansion, and market share, but its wider significance lies in the opportunities it creates. Can employees build secure futures for their families? Can smaller suppliers participate in the value chain?
Can more Filipinos access education, livelihoods, and the resources they need to thrive? These questions bring social impact closer to the core of business strategy.

The launch of Ventures for a More Humane World: A Handbook for Social Entrepreneurs in the Philippines, by Dr. Raymund Habaradas and Professor Ian Benedict Mia, reinforced the importance of equipping enterprises to turn their intentions into practice. Social entrepreneurship requires more than compassion; it needs knowledge, viable business models, and a supportive network that allows solutions to endure and grow.

Ultimately, rethinking enterprise does not mean treating profit as the enemy of social progress. Profit can sustain an organization, fund innovation, and extend its reach. The question is whether these capabilities serve a purpose beyond accumulation alone. When businesses take responsibility for the effects of their decisions, success becomes more than an internal achievement: it becomes a means of creating opportunities for others.
The challenge is not simply to declare that business should be a force for good. It is to make that commitment visible in how capital is invested, people are treated, and growth is pursued.
For every business leader, the question remains: “What need can our business meet, and how can our success help others thrive?” – Rappler.com

Madriella L. Mendoza is the Communications/Business Development Officer of the PHINMA–DLSU Center for Business and Society. She works on communications, public relations, business development, and initiatives that advance the Center’s mission of promoting business as a force for good. She may be reached at madriella.mendoza@dlsu.edu.ph.

articles.title: No talks about VP Sara replacement amid impeachment trial --Palace
articles.summary: Thoughts of a possible replacement for Vice President Sara Duterte amid the ongoing impeachment trial is far from President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr's mind, according to Palace Press Officer…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 10:16am

Thoughts of a possible replacement for Vice President Sara Duterte amid the ongoing impeachment trial is far from President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr's mind, according to Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro.
"Hindi po naiisip ng Pangulo yan, sa totoo. Hindi po napaguusapan. Sa ngayon, kahit kami ay nag-memeeeting, hindi napaguusapan ang impeachment," Castro said in an interview on Unang Balita on Friday.
(The President doesn't actually think about that, to be honest. It’s not being discussed. Even when we hold meetings, impeachment is not brought up.)
"Ang nais lang po talaga niya ay due process," Castro added.
(All he really wants is due process.)
Previously, Malacañang also said that nobody will interfere with Duterte's decision to remain on her post amid her impeachment trial.
Duterte on Tuesday said she "will not resign, will never resign from the Office of the Vice President" amid her impeachment trial and the allegations against her.
"Kung hindi po siya magre-resign, desisyon niya po 'yan. Walang manghihimasok diyan. Pero ang pagsasabi niya na mag-resign ang Pangulo, 'yan ay malaking kalokohan," she added.
(If she chooses not to resign, that is her decision. No one will interfere with that. But for her to say that the President should resign, that is utter nonsense.)
Articles of impeachment

On Tuesday the House prosecution panel dropped three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Duterte, saying its case will stand on Article II alone on alleged unexplained wealth due to non-full declaration of assets and non-divestment of business.
Duterte's camp said the prosecution's withdrawal of three articles of impeachment os an admission that the allegations hurled against her lacked basis.
Duterte's camp has criticized the move of the prosecutors.
Castro, however, asked why the defense team did not object to the dropping of the articles.
"Ang pagbitiw sa articles of impeachment, hindi naman natin nakitaan ng objection yung defense team, nagbigay lang sila ng manifestation. But the team did not give any objection," said Castro.
(Regarding the withdrawal of the articles of impeachment, we did not see any objection from the defense team; they merely had a manifestation. But the team did not raise any objection.)

"So, parang wala naman dapat sisihin dito, kasi parang sinisisi nila ang prosecution, yung senador judges, poero kung babasahin mo lahat, mapapanood mo lahat ng hearing, wala tayong marririnig na objection, iba yung objection sa manifestation," she added.

(So, it seems there’s no one to blame here—though it appears they are blaming the prosecution and the senator-judges—but if you read everything and watch all the hearings, you won’t hear any objections; an objection is different from a manifestation.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: What is lung adenocarcinoma, the cancer diagnosed in Pope Leo?
articles.summary: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, often found in non-smokers and typically grows slowly

blocks.text: PRAY. A woman holds a rosary and a card portraying Pope Leo outside Gemelli Hospital, where the Pontiff is being treated for lung cancer following surgery to remove part of his right lung, in Rome, Italy, October 14, 2026. REUTERS/Yara Nardi
Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, often found in non-smokers and typically grows slowly

items: Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after surgery to remove a lobe of his lung.
Prognosis depends on the cancer's stage and spread, with treatment options including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
VATICAN – Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during surgery on Tuesday, the Vatican said.
Here are some facts about the disease.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer that forms in glandular cells, which produce substances such as mucus. In the lungs, it develops in cells lining the air sacs and is the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the category that accounts for about 80%-85% of lung cancers. Adenocarcinoma represents roughly 40% of all lung cancer cases, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo back on his feet after shock cancer diagnosis

blocks.text: It is typically found in the outer parts of the lungs and tends to grow more slowly than some other forms of lung cancer, increasing the chances of detection before it has spread.
Smoking remains the main risk factor. However, adenocarcinoma is also the most common type of lung cancer among people who have never smoked. The pope is not known to have been a smoker.

Early-stage disease often causes no symptoms and may be discovered during scans performed for other reasons. As the cancer progresses, symptoms can include a persistent cough, shortness of breath or wheezing, coughing up blood, chest, shoulder or back pain, unexplained weight loss and fatigue.
The Vatican has said the tumor was found during a routine health check. Leo said on Sunday that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
For patients whose cancer is confined to the lung, surgery offers the best chance of a cure.

The standard operation is a lobectomy, as occurred on Tuesday, in which an entire lobe of the lung is removed. Doctors consider it the preferred treatment when the tumor is limited to a single lobe because it maximizes the chances of removing all cancerous tissue while preserving as much lung function as possible.

Depending on the stage of the disease, treatment can also include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted drugs and immunotherapy. The Vatican has not given any information yet on what follow-up treatment the pope might need.
Doctors say prognosis depends heavily on the stage of the cancer and whether it has spread beyond the lung.
The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumor or whether lymph nodes were affected, making it impossible to assess Leo’s individual prognosis at this stage.

According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year relative survival rate for non-small cell lung cancer is 67% when the disease remains confined to the lung. The rate falls to about 40% when the disease has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes and to about 12% when it has spread to distant organs.

However, it says people being diagnosed now may have a better outlook than these statistics suggest because of improving treatments. Medical experts also caution that outcomes vary widely depending on tumor size, lymph node involvement, a patient’s age and overall health.
(This factbox drew on information posted online by the Lung Cancer Foundation of America, the National Library of Medicine and the American Cancer Society.) – Rappler.com

A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting. The indictment of 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country means there is probable cause for prosecutors to pursue the case.
U.S. Department of Justice says the indictment details acts taken to further February school shooting
A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting.
The indictment of 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country means there is probable cause for prosecutors to pursue the case.
Emily Langlie, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said last week that an indictment would mean a preliminary hearing in the case scheduled for Oct. 20 would be eliminated.
Bryant, whose lawyers say uses she/her pronouns and goes by the name Melody, was denied bail a day ahead of Wednesday's indictment.
U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter
A statement issued by the U.S. Department of Justice says the indictment "details several overt acts that Bryant took to further the school shooting conspiracy."
Eight victims were shot dead in Tumbler Ridge by 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar in February, including five students and a teacher at a secondary school.

The indictment of Bellingham, Wash., resident Bryant lists that she allegedly agreed to record the shooting and broadcast it over the internet, offered the shooter advice on where to attack and what weapons to use and sent Van Rootselaar money to buy a lighter for use in an improvised explosive device.

items: Pope Leo is recovering well from lung cancer surgery, having begun walking and eating normally, with doctors reporting positive post-operative results.
World leaders and Catholics are offering prayers for his recovery, while his upcoming tour of South America remains planned, though dates may change based on his health.

The pope's surgery involved the removal of part of his lung, and while the prognosis depends on whether the cancer has spread, specialists suggest the operation may be curative if no further issues arise.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

VATICAN – Pope Leo‘s recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room and eating normally, the Vatican said on Wednesday, after doctors announced the 71-year-old pontiff was being treated for lung cancer.
World leaders, Catholics across the globe and senior cardinals at the Vatican have offered prayers for Leo after he had part of his right lung removed in an operation on Tuesday, October 13.
Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on Wednesday, October 14, showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said, adding that the pontiff had undergone respiratory physiotherapy.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo had peaceful night in hospital after lung cancer surgery

blocks.text: The cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

Leo normally follows a very busy schedule. He is due to make a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17 and the Vatican press office said on Wednesday that “nothing has changed” regarding the planned trip.
However, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said on Wednesday that the dates could change because of the amount of time his recovery would take.

blocks.caption: What is lung adenocarcinoma, the cancer diagnosed in Pope Leo?

blocks.text: The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican’s vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.
A prayer was recited for Leo to have a good convalescence and complete healing during an open-air Mass in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday following the surgery.

The pope has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during Tuesday’s operation in an effort to eliminate all cancerous tissue.
Human lungs have five lobes — three in the right lung and two in the left.

The operation lasted about 90 minutes and was completed without complications, the pope’s lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, said late on Tuesday.
The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.

Dr. Serena Ricciardi, a lung cancer specialist at Rome’s San Camillo Forlanini Hospital, said that if the cancer had not spread to Leo’s lymph nodes, the surgery may have been sufficient for treatment.
“If there are no further issues or lymph node involvement, we could consider the surgery curative,” she told Reuters. “The disease has been completely removed.”
Leo is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.
The Vatican said this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and that all his public engagements had been canceled until October 20.
The Mass on Wednesday was the closing act of an assembly of bishops called by Leo to discuss the Church’s family life teachings, the largest gathering of Church leaders so far during this papacy.

Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle led the service in place of Leo. The pope last week approved Tagle as the dean of the Church’s College of Cardinals, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to the elite role.
Political leaders offered messages of support.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife Jeanette were praying for the pope, an American who was born in Chicago.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” he said on X. Rubio met Leo at the Vatican in May.
US President Donald Trump, who has criticized the Roman Catholic Church leader, said on Wednesday he hoped that Pope Leo would “get better fast.”
“I want to see Pope Leo get well,” Trump told reporters. “I just want to wish him well, get better fast.” – Rappler.com
