articles.title: Labor and Coalition set to reject bill to stop incarcerated women being shackled in childbirth
articles.summary:
Liberal Paul Scarr breaks ranks to condemn major parties, saying he will write to Queensland attorney general

Labor and the Coalition are set to reject a bill that would have banned the…

blocks.text: Labor and the Coalition have blocked a vote on a bill that would have banned the shackling of incarcerated women during childbirth, with the government saying it was the responsibility of the states and territories.
Independent senator Lidia Thorpe introduced the bills into the Senate, which would prevent shackling and stop children being strip-searched.
“In 2026 people can be shackled while giving birth, and children can can also have their clothes removed by adults to examine their bodies legally,” Thorpe told the Senate.
“The people sitting in this room have the power to end these barbaric, inhumane traumatic and totally unnecessary practices.”

The government said “the responsibility of criminal justice system predominantly sits with state and territory governments”, while the Coalition said it “understands the intent” of the bill but also would not support its passage.

Queensland Liberal senator Paul Scarr broke ranks to condemn the major parties, describing himself as “deeply concerned” by the Australia-wide practice and vowing to raise it with the Queensland attorney general, Deb Frecklington.
He urged the prime minister to convene a national cabinet meeting.

“What I’ve heard deeply concerns me and I do hope, that this vote shouldn’t be an end to this matter, we’ve got to do better than this and we’ve got to look at ways this issue can be addressed,” Scarr said.
The only data on giving birth while incarcerated was from 2017, when 25 women gave birth.

Fifteen years ago, the UN general assembly adopted the Bangkok Rules on the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”.
The rules were adopted unanimously by the general assembly. But around the world, they are regularly flouted.
Greens leader, David Shoebridge, was scathing of the two major parties in rejecting the bill.

“The Labor party and the Coalition come in here and say it’s a matter for states and territories if they want to shackle women to a bed while they’re giving birth we’ll just let them do that,” he told the Senate. “Don’t torture women giving birth and don’t strip-search children.”

articles.title: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia faces mounting questions about resume

image.caption: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is seen in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. Zacharia is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
The new White House press secretary is facing mounting questions about her background and resume as she transitions into her role as the public face of the Trump administration.
No evidence so far that self-described lawyer has passed any state's bar exam

Katie Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer as she has worked to establish herself as a commentator for conservative outlets like Fox News and Newsmax. But so far, she and the White House have offered no evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.

The questions add to the confusion surrounding U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to hire Zacharia, who had worked for his social media company for only a few months when he announced her appointment and whose debut at the podium on Tuesday has been widely panned.

Afterward, the president was asked by reporters where Zacharia had passed the bar exam, following a report by the independent outlet Popular Information that she did not appear to be licensed in any state.
Trump stepped aside to allow Zacharia to answer.
"When I moved to China," she responded over the sound of Marine One whirring in the background. It is not clear what she had intended to say or whether she had finished the sentence.
New White House press secretary stumbles in first briefing | Hanomansing Live
China's notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination can only be taken by Chinese citizens.

Asked what credentials she held, the White House passed along a statement from Zacharia, who received a bachelor of arts degree from Pepperdine University in 2007 and received her law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, according to the school and her LinkedIn bio.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," it read.

Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, added that Zacharia was "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary."

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia has been the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media & Technology Group since June and spent two months as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.
U.S. President Donald Trump is seen speaking with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday, with Zacharia looking on from nearby. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

From 2011 to 2013, it says, she served as an associate on the international practice team at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing. She also worked as the manager of fundraising and communications for Compassion for Migrant Children, which assists the children of migrant workers, from 2012 to 2013.
More recently, it says she served as general counsel for Fix California, a group started by Trump administration official Richard Grenell.
Neither the firm nor the two groups responded to questions about her tenure and background.
On Instagram, Zacharia describes herself as the White House press secretary, "Wife, Mom, & Lawyer" (with four heart emojis after "Mom").

And her official author page at the California Globe, where she wrote occasional commentary, says that, in addition to being a "regular commentator on Fox News, Newsmax," she has "extensive experience in political advocacy, international corporate law, and non-profit work, including time as outside counsel for the World Bank and IFC in Beijing."

items: Zacharia fails to impress in brief debut as White House press secretary
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave job at month's end, Trump says

blocks.text: A June 2026 press release from NovaRed Mining Inc. announcing her appointment to the company's advisory board, which was first reported by Popular Information, said her "professional experience includes work related to international legal and financial transactions, including matters involving organizations associated with the World Bank Group and the International Finance Corporation during her tenure with Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing."

In announcing her hire on his social media site, Trump described Zacharia as "a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney, and a frequent Commentator on outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax."
"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" he added.
Not listed with state bar
Zacharia is not listed as a member of the state bar in California, where she currently resides, according to a public database.

Rick Coca, a spokesperson for the State Bar of California, the regulatory agency that oversees state licensing, said in a statement that it has "no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black" or any version of her married or maiden names "having been licensed to practice law in California."
Popular Information said the same was the case in all 50 states it had queried, plus Washington, D.C.

In response, the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability (CfA) filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California asking it to investigate whether Zacharia misrepresented herself as a lawyer in violation of California law.

"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has," said CfA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith in a statement.
The State Bar said it could not confirm whether it had received the complaint or were conducting an investigation, citing confidentiality laws.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Semirara: The government is auctioning an energy crisis
articles.summary: The government’s pursuit of the highest financial offer may inadvertently trigger the Philippines' most expensive energy failure

blocks.text: As the government prepares to auction the Semirara coal mine to the highest bidder, its focus on maximizing state revenues over technical competence threatens to trigger a national energy crisis. With the Acacia pit rapidly flooding with seawater and production targets drastically slashed, handing the operation to a new contractor unprepared for this severe engineering failure risks forcing electricity consumers, displaced workers, and the local economy to absorb the catastrophic cost of regulatory negligence.

The Philippine government unequivocally possesses the right to demand a superior return from the vast coal reserves of Semirara Island. These vital natural resources belong fundamentally to the state, not to the incumbent operator, Semirara Mining and Power Corp. (SMPC). It is thus prudent for regulators to reassess the terms as Coal Operating Contract No. 5 approaches its July 14, 2027, expiration.

However, in its eagerness to maximize state revenues, the Department of Energy (DOE) appears to be losing sight of a crucial engineering reality: an auction is only as valuable as the asset that can be operated.

If the winning bidder cannot immediately master a rapidly flooding pit, mobilize highly specialized equipment, retain a massive workforce, and continuously produce coal, the government’s pursuit of the highest financial offer will inadvertently trigger the nation’s most expensive energy failure.
The rapidly deteriorating physical condition of the mine makes the demand for absolute transparency not just urgent, but critical to our national energy security.

SMPC has disclosed that seawater is currently surging into the Acacia mine at an astonishing rate of approximately 30,000 cubic meters an hour. To put this catastrophic volume into perspective, it is equivalent to 12 Olympic-size swimming pools flooding the active mining site every single hour—a deluge that now vastly exceeds the mine’s existing pumping capacity.

The structural integrity of the site is already failing under this pressure. On September 20, dumped and in-situ material from North Block 1 Dam 2 completely collapsed, dangerously redirecting surface runoff directly toward the pit.
Consequently, crucial stripping operations in Acacia have been indefinitely suspended while SMPC scrambles to construct another cut-off wall and undertakes emergency remedial work.

This structural failure is profoundly alarming because the Acacia pit had been heavily relied upon to supply the vast majority of the company’s projected coal production in 2027. Are regulators preparing to hand over a lucrative natural resource, or are they blindly auctioning a poisoned chalice?

The human and production consequences resulting from this operational crisis are already highly measurable and accelerating. Initially, SMPC announced sudden redundancies affecting 462 mine-site employees, but the situation quickly worsened, leading the company to add another 996 workers to the chopping block, bringing the total to a staggering 1,458 displaced individuals.

Furthermore, its revised 2026 production target has been slashed to just 12 million metric tons, representing a precipitous drop of nearly 40% below the record 19.9 million tons the company produced in 2025.

SMPC claims that lingering uncertainty over the upcoming contract severely complicates any further investments in the massive pumps, power systems, and supporting infrastructure required to save the pit.

While that explanation is financially plausible from a corporate standpoint, it does not absolve SMPC of its underlying responsibility to explain exactly how the mine was allowed to reach this precarious, flooded condition under its watch, nor does it clarify how much the required remediation will ultimately cost the next operator.

The collateral economic damage is swiftly moving far beyond the company’s immediate payroll. It was reported than on October 11, Island entrepreneur Janice Lim had already experienced slower sales, fewer customers, and delayed payments as workers grew increasingly terrified about their immediate job security.

At the Divine Word School of Semirara Island, where SMPC historically provides approximately P90 million annually for free tuition and the education of employees’ children, more than 1,500 students now face a completely uncertain future, according to the student-government president.

These accounts make one point unmistakable: a credible transition plan crafted by the government must robustly protect households, schools, and small businesses, rather than merely keeping a lucrative mine permit alive on paper.

This brings us to the glaring issue of regulatory negligence. The DOE prudently terminated the earlier bid round in September following the initial seawater problem, ongoing legal disputes, and mounting stakeholder concerns, stating that a new auction would seek greater government revenue, domestic coal commitments, and enhanced consumer benefits. But restarting this complex process in November or December leaves barely seven months before the contract’s expiry.

A new operator would have to seamlessly arrange billions in financing, secure specialized equipment, recruit and train thousands of workers, master a highly complex mine plan, and assume control of a pit that is actively sinking.

The governance problem surrounding this transition is becoming significantly harder to defend. SMPC states that the regulatory process has produced no bid bulletins, no prequalification screening, no model contract, and no official answers to its vital technical questions—even as the highest financial offer, rather than demonstrated mining competence and engineering capability, remains the sole determinant of the winner.

When more than P55 billion in existing mine investments, thousands of local jobs, and critical domestic coal production are exposed to this level of uncertainty, procedural silence from the DOE morphs into a severe public-interest risk.

This dispute is further complicated by a contentious court case over the heavy equipment and infrastructure already situated on Semirara Island. SMPC filed a petition for declaratory relief after the DOE demanded a full inventory of its property, plant, and equipment, stating this proprietary information would be made available to competing bidders.

blocks.caption: Semirara takes DOE data dispute to court amid race for biggest coal mine

blocks.text: The DOE maintains that assets whose costs have been recovered—and materials not removed within one year after contract termination—may vest in the government and be made available to the eventual winner. SMPC firmly argues that cost recovery is merely reimbursement, not a transfer of ownership, and relies on Presidential Decree 972 to preserve its absolute title and removal rights.

SMPC highlights that it paid an impressive P43.4 billion in government share and P3.7 billion in taxes from 2021 through the first half of 2026. Those figures should absolutely be independently verified, but the company’s shutdown warnings should not simply frighten the government into granting a perpetual, automatic extension.

The government has no mandate to unconditionally preserve SMPC’s incumbency. It must, however, prove that replacing the operator—or retaining it through a genuinely competitive bidding process—will successfully protect the grid, public revenues, and operating continuity.

An incumbent’s experience creates a natural advantage, not a permanent entitlement. But neither should the government confuse a large financial bid with the actual technical ability to operate an unusually difficult, failing mine.
The public-interest solution is to make the competition truly real and grounded in engineering reality.

The DOE must comprehensively disclose the scoring system, require minimum experience, verify committed technical personnel, and explicitly outline the financial consequences if the winner fails to keep the water out.

Until these fundamental questions are fully answered, the government is not simply auctioning coal; it is auctioning an impending energy cost shock and unfairly forcing electricity consumers to absorb the catastrophic risk. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ombudsman grants over 1,600 SALN requests in a year
articles.summary: In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the Office of the Ombudsman said that it has granted 1655 SALN requests.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 7:44am
Office of the Ombudsman along Agham Road in Quezon City.
Wikipedia / patrickroque01

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has granted more than 1,600 requests for Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) a year after the anti-graft office lifted the restrictions on access to these documents by the media and the public.
In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the Office of the Ombudsman said that it had granted 1,655 SALN requests.
“One of my first acts as Ombudsman was to tear down the barriers to the Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth of public officials,” Remulla said in a statement.
“For years, the public was told to ask the official's permission before seeing what that official owned. We ended that,” he added.
Remulla also stressed that making government officials' financial disclosures accessible to the public is vital to maintaining transparency and accountability.
“Ang yaman ng isang lingkod-bayan ay hindi pribadong usapin. Kapag pera ng bayan ang pinag-uusapan, may karapatan ang bayan na malaman,” he said.
(The wealth of a public servant is not a private matter. When it comes to the people's money, the people have a right to know.)
On Oct. 14, 2025, then newly appointed Ombudsman Remulla lifted the restriction on SALN access imposed by former Ombudsman Samuel Martires.
The previous requirement for access to an official’s SALN barred the public and the media from obtaining copies of officials’ disclosures without a notarized letter of authority from the declarant.

blocks.text: North Korea said Wednesday it test-fired cruise missiles designed to be fired from submarines to test the readiness of the country's underwater combat systems and strengthen the Navy's capabilities.
North Korea's state media said it carried out the tests in waters off the east coast of the Korean peninsula.
A North Korean state media report described the weapons as strategic, implying an intent to arm them with nuclear warheads.
But the report did not specify whether they were launched from an actual submarine or an underwater test platform.
North Korea has pushed ahead with modern missile submarines and both ballistic and cruise missile developments.

blocks.caption: People in South Korea watching the news about North Korea having fired ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on October 12Image: Kim Hong-Ji/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pyongyang has tested various weapons in recent weeks to sharpen its military deterrence against the United States and South Korea, but it is not ​yet believed to ‌have launched a modern missile submarine in full operation.
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
What to know about North Korea's relations with South Korea and the US

The latest development comes two days after the North Korean state media released photos of the North Korean leader, Kim Jong Un, visiting a new military museum in an undisclosed location in the country.
The museum displayed an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of reaching the US, photos released by KNCA state media showed.
Kim has made clear that boosting his country's nuclear arsenal was his key priority. Denuclearization, as the US has pushed for, is off the table in this case.
Relations between the North Korean leader and US President Donald Trump also appear to have quieted since the two haven't met in recent years.
US President Donald Trump, during his first term, met Kim three times. Earlier in the week, Trump, alluding to a trip to Asia next month, said he might meet Kim on the trip.
North Korea has put a halt to all coordination with South Korea and has removed all references to reunification with the South from its constitution.

articles.title: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago
articles.summary:
Alleged assault follows report of gang rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online

A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at…

blocks.text: A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago, as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.
The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence, according to a university daily crime log.
In a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.
She told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.
A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.
The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, they announced on Wednesday.
No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.
Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.

“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.
“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”

The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.
New York state prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the report.
Under mounting backlash, Cornell has also suspended all fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.

Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, including accusations of a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.

articles.title: Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest
articles.summary: Real estate developer Sacha Singh tells a Toronto court he gave self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski more than $4.5 million to trade in foreign exchange and cryptocurrency. That’s more than…

image.caption: Sacha Singh, right, testifies by video at the fraud trial of self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski on Wednesday. The real estate developer invested more than $4.5 million with Pleterski between April 2021 and January 2022. (Pam Davies/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Real estate developer Sacha Singh tells a Toronto court he gave self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski more than $4.5 million to trade in foreign exchange and cryptocurrency. That’s more than any of the 11 investors who’ve been called so far as Crown witnesses at Pleterski’s fraud trial. Most say they never got any money back.
'I thought he was a sharp kid,' Sacha Singh tells Toronto jury

One of the self-described "Crypto King's" largest investors testified Wednesday about how Aiden Pleterski was touted as the "next big thing" and that he'd heard about others getting paid returns before he began investing thousands and later millions of dollars with him.
Real estate developer Sacha Singh, who testified virtually at Pleterski's fraud trial in Toronto, said he first met the now-27-year-old at a restaurant in Pickering, Ont., in the spring of 2021.
"I know a lot of big entrepreneurs in the crypto space are younger kids," Singh told the jury in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice.
"I thought he was a sharp kid and could be one of those unicorns."

Singh signed a contract for his first investment of $10,000 cash that April. From there, the court was shown 22 more investment contracts between Singh and Pleterski totalling more than $4.5 million over the next 10 months.
Wire transfer receipts were shown for most of the contracts, which ranged from $10,000 to $1.3 million, but a few others included notes they were paid in cash.
Pleterski is representing himself at his fraud and money laundering trial before the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. (Aiden Pleterski/Instagram/Durham Regional Police)

That's the most money any of the 11 investors who've been called as Crown witnesses, so far, have said they gave him to trade on their behalf. Combined, the other 10 testified they provided Pleterski with roughly $2.3 million. Most have said they never got any of their money back.
Pleterski is representing himself at trial and has pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering.

The Crown is alleging Pleterski guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds. Instead, the Crown argues Pleterski spent the money on himself, including on exotic cars, flights on private jets, lavish shopping and credit card bills that ran into the millions.
Thought investment grew to $26M

Singh was introduced to Pleterski by another investor, Akil Heywood. Like many investors who've testified in the case, Singh said Pleterski would message him his weekly percentage gains from Pleterski's trading in foreign exchange and cryptocurrency.
Singh, left, testified that another investor, Akil Heywood, right, introduced him to Pleterski. (Atlantic Mas Toronto/Facebook)

Singh kept a spreadsheet of those returns, which was shown in court. By March 2022, his calculations on the weekly gains, which ranged from three to nearly 11 per cent, showed his investment had grown to more than $26 million.
Though he never received those returns — nor most of what he invested — Singh is one of the few investors who says he did receive some money back from Pleterski.

items: ‘Crypto King’ investors testify they gave Aiden Pleterski a total $1.9M as trial continues
'Crypto King' investor who lost $890K recounts visit to Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion

blocks.text: He testified he only continued investing because he received $700,000 back when he asked to withdraw a million dollars in November 2021. The other $300,000 went to Pleterski as his fee for trading as laid out in the investment contracts.
"If you knew the source of that $700,000 was just money you already gave to him, would you have continued to invest with him?" Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson asked Singh in court.
"No," he replied.
'Selling assets'
Eventually though, Singh suspected Pleterski hadn't made that money trading.

He recorded several phone calls with Pleterski about a year after his initial investment. By then, Singh testified Pleterski "essentially ghosted" him when he asked to withdraw a large sum from his investment, which was supposed to be traded through a platform called FXChoice.

In one of the recordings heard in court from around April 2022, Singh asks Pleterski "that 700,000 you gave me, did that come from FXChoice? Or did that come from other investors that gave you money and you just gave it to me?"

Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson, right, asked Singh if he would have invested with Pleterski if he knew the money he got back was the same money Singh gave Pleterski to invest. Singh said no. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Pleterski tells him that it did come from that trading platform, but that since February 2022, he had been paying returns from his "own pocket" because, Pleterski said, FXChoice wasn't paying him out.

In other recordings Singh took, Pleterski also blames FXChoice for issues paying investors —claiming the platform only has access to a total of $20-$30 million — and elaborates on how he's been using his own money to pay returns.

"I'm actually selling assets to be able to pay people back because I feel like I have an obligation to do so," Pleterski tells Singh. "I've pretty much been paying people out of pocket for months and months … and I can't afford to keep doing that."

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski spent investors' money on exotic cars, private jet flights: Crown
'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn’t exist

blocks.text: Around this time, Singh testified he was also shown a video Pleterski took of the FXChoice account, showing there was more than $311 million in it.
The video was shown to him by Mitchell Learning, another investor who testified last week.
Learning told the court about how he went looking for "proof in person" of how much money was in Pleterski's investment account — after receiving a screenshot and video showing that same balance.
Mitchell Learning, a former friend and investor of Pleterski's, testified last week. (Mehrdad Nazarahar/CBC)

Learning went to Pleterski's lakefront mansion in Burlington, Ont., in June 2022 and was able to access Pleterski's email account on his computer. He testified that he found an email from FXChoice confirming Pleterski had deleted that account.
That same day, Learning said he confronted Pleterski and was told "a story" that everything had been going well until the summer of 2021, "where apparently things took a turn."
Admits to Ponzi scheme
According to Learning's testimony, Pleterski told him that, by around that September, he had only $40 million in a trading account.

"It only kept going down from there," Learning said, continuing to recount Pleterski's story. "He tried to make riskier trades to make money back, essentially losing the remainder of the money and then from that point on starting running a Ponzi scheme."
Pleterski didn't cross-examine Learning or Singh. So far, he's only cross-examined the first investor witness the Crown has called.
Pleterski is representing himself in court. So far, he's only cross-examined one of a dozen Crown witnesses called in his case. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
"I don't have the legal knowledge to challenge the inconsistencies, your honour," he said Wednesday, when asked by Justice Shaun Nakatsuru if he had questions for Singh.
Pleterski was arrested in May 2024 after a lengthy investigation by Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission. Police allege he operated a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme.
His trial is expected to continue Friday.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: Rapper-economist Cielo Magno confirms she will run for Senate
articles.summary: Will anti-corruption crusader Cielo Magno succeed where former NEDA chief Winnie Monsod failed?

blocks.text: PROF. Economics Professor Cielo Magno speaks before religious and civil groups gathered at EDSA Shrine, calling for the impeachment of Vice President Sara Duterte, on January 31, 2025.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
Will anti-corruption crusader Cielo Magno succeed where former NEDA chief Winnie Monsod failed?

items: Cielo Magno, an economist and former undersecretary at the Department of Finance, announced her candidacy for the Senate in the 2028 elections during a forum in Italy.
Magno, who has been vocal about socio-economic reforms and has a significant social media following, aims to connect with younger voters through her music and digital content.
Despite her strong advocacy and background, Magno faces challenges in raising her public awareness and competing against established candidates in a crowded Senate race.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Twenty-five years after UP economist Solita “Winnie” Monsod’s failed bid for a Senate seat, another teacher of the UP School of Economics is giving the Senate a shot.
Economist Cielo Magno announced in a forum with Filipinos in Italy this week that she will run for senator in the 2028 elections.
“Yes, po, I’m running for senator in 2028,” said the 48-year-old academic in response to a question posed to her during the forum.

Magno served as undersecretary for fiscal policy and monitoring group of the Department of Finance for over a year but was “terminated” by Malacañang in September 2023 after she indirectly questioned President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s policy to set a price ceiling on rice amid rising prices.

I knew when I posted the supply and demand graph that my boss would receive a call from Malacañang to remove me, but I did it anyway. With how things were going, I knew it was time to go. pic.twitter.com/WKGBXjdiK9— Cielo Magno (@profcielomagno) September 9, 2023

Magno had posted on her personal social media account the chart on the law of supply and demand and said “I miss teaching,” in an apparent criticism of Marcos’ price cap on the basic staple via his Executive Order No. 39.
Magno’s immediate boss at the time, then-finance secretary Benjamin Diokno, had backed the price controls on rice.

Days after she left the department, Magno said: “It is our responsibility as civil servants to say if a policy is flawed. It’s very dangerous to just say ‘yes’ because we don’t want to offend the boss. Policies have real consequences on people’s lives. They have to be well thought out.”

Magno returned to her alma mater, the UP School of Economics, to teach. She finished her Bachelor of Science in Business Economics and her Master of Arts in Economics from the state university. She has since been active in pushing for socio-economic reforms such as budget transparency, and political reforms such as a law against political dynasties. She was also among those who lobbied against defunding PhilHealth, in a petition that was won in the Supreme Court in December 2025.

Since leaving government two years ago, Magno has become a digital creator and has built a respectable following on social media. She now has over 204k followers on Facebook; 107k followers on YouTube; and 141k followers on TikTok.

blocks.caption: Rapper-economist Cielo Magno confirms she will run for Senate

blocks.text: Magno is also a musician: she sings, raps, and plays the saxophone. She composed with Jake Regala the now-famous anti-corruption song, “Tax ng Ina Mo, Bantayan Mo,” which she has performed in various protest activities on the flood control corruption scandal, including the Trillion Peso March at the People Power Monument on November 30, 2025.

blocks.caption: Rapper-economist Cielo Magno confirms she will run for Senate

blocks.text: On her YouTube account, the “Tax ng Ina Mo” video has at least 105k views. The karaoke version of the video on her account has 4,700 views, but many others have posted their own renditions of the song.

In a bid to reach out to the younger generation, Magno has uploaded a rap video series titled “Unrap da Kurap: Bugtong raps,” with critical lyrics about fugitive Senator Bato dela Rosa, convicted preacher Apollo Quiboloy, and Vice President Sara Duterte, among others.

blocks.caption: Rapper-economist Cielo Magno confirms she will run for Senate

blocks.text: She has received several recognitions since leaving government including The Outstanding Women in the Nation’s Service or TOWNS award in 2025 for her contributions to financial accountability and good governance.

It is rare for academics with no political pedigree to join the Senate race. Graduates of the UP School of Economics are usually tapped to become technocrats and serve in offices such as the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (formerly NEDA) or the Department of Finance.

Monsod, now professor emeritus of the UP School of Economics, tried in 2001 when she ran as a candidate of Aksyon Demokratiko in the People Power Coalition of then-newly installed president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo but didn’t make it. Back then, she was a television personality known as “Mareng Winnie.” She has had a number of public affairs shows on GMA Network through the years, and has also served on the board of Rappler.
Magno will have to overcome her comparatively low awareness among the masses who comprise the majority of the Filipino electorate.

Filipino voters typically choose incumbents or returning senators for the Senate and since there are only 12 seats up for grabs, the chances of new candidates winning are quite low as dozens of candidates fight for the last few slots.

In the latest publicly available Pulse Asia survey on the 2028 senatorial race conducted from September 17 to 24, 2026, only 12% of survey respondents were aware of Magno. With 66 names on the list, she would have placed anywhere from 48th to 66th if the elections were held last month, with only 0.7% of respondents voting for her.

blocks.caption: Image from Pulse Asia’s October 12, 2026 media release.

blocks.text: Magno, however, has some strong points. She is from the vote-rich region of Central Luzon, with Nueva Ecija as her home province.

She will likely be backed by the left-leaning citizens’ party Akbayan, which pulled a surprise in the 2025 elections by topping the party-list race and winning 3 seats. If her low awareness rating doesn’t improve, she could follow the footsteps of Akbayan Representative Chel Diokno, who iniitially planned a third bid for a Senate seat (after two tries) in 2025 but opted instead to join the party-list race as first nominee of Akbayan.

Being a musician and rapper, Magno may be able to connect with young voters who make up the majority of the electorate. She will, however, have to do a lot more work in improving her awareness rating via traditional and new media.
Asked in Italy what she’ll focus on if she wins, Magno said she will continue her advocacy of reforming the national budget, especially with respect to health care, and pushing for industrial policy.
“Ang tinututukan ko talaga sa budget ay yung health care… So sa akin po, napakahalaga ng health care system,” she said.
(My focus on the budget is health care… In my view, the healthcare system is very important.)

blocks.caption: COUPLE. Economics Professor Cielo Magno with husband Dante “Dan” Gatmaytan, a faculty member of the UP College of Law, during the TOWNS awarding ceremony in October 2025. Cielo Magno Facebook.

blocks.text: Magno is married to UP College of Law Professor Dante Gatmaytan. They have a son, Samuel. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Stopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktank
articles.summary:
Resolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to work

Banning people with anxiety, ADHD or autism from claiming disability benefits…

blocks.text: Banning people with anxiety, ADHD or autism from claiming disability benefits would not deliver major financial savings and would probably make it harder for them to get or stay in a job and participate in society, a leading thinktank has warned.

The Resolution Foundation said any proposals to make certain mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions ineligible for personal independence payments (Pip) would be “crude changes” aimed at hitting unrealistic savings targets.

But it warned that Pip was “failing on several fronts” and called for a major overhaul to keep a lid on costs – currently rising at an “unsustainable” rate – and restore public trust in a benefit widely seen as unfair and dysfunctional.

About £4.4bn a year could be saved if Pip support was better targeted, it said. Cash support could be removed from an estimated one in six working-age Pip claimants (670,000) who report having no extra costs as a result of their disability.

However, it added that any reforms should proceed with caution because of the success of Pip in ensuring high numbers of disabled and ill people were able to participate in “economically valuable” activities, such as work, caring, training or volunteering, that they would not be able to do otherwise.

Official concern over Pip has soared in recent years, in part because of the rapidly rising number of claimants, particularly among young people, with much of that sharp increase linked to claims for mental health, ADHD and autism.

Spending on Pip in England and Wales has risen in real terms by 183% since it was introduced in 2014. This year the bill is expected to be £28bn, rising to £34bn by the end of the decade, according to official forecasts.

Attempts by the previous Labour administration under Keir Starmer to push through £5bn of crude savings to Pip collapsed last year amid a rebellion of backbench MPs. His successor, Andy Burnham, has said renewed attempts to reform benefits would not involve “crude cuts”.

Welfare officials, who are awaiting an official review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timms and the Milburn review of the youth jobs crisis, are understood to be considering proposals to exclude under-25s from the Pip system.

Pip has also found itself at the heart of culture war rows, with some, such as the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, arguing it should not be paid to claimants with so-called “mild” conditions that were not disabling or likely to incur higher daily living costs.

The Resolution Foundation said attempting to link Pip awards to particular conditions was simplistic and impractical as most claimants reported multiple conditions – often combining physical, mental and behavioural conditions.

Lindsay Judge, the thinktank’s research director, said: “Pip is a vital benefit for disabled people that enables them to participate in society and live fuller and more active lives. But the current system is failing on several fronts – claimants don’t trust it, awards don’t fully reflect the nature of disability today and spending is rising unsustainably.

“As well as continuing to provide cash awards to help with ongoing additional costs, a reformed Pip system should focus on supporting disabled people to participate in society. A system more attuned to people’s needs would also mean that around one in six current Pip recipients who don’t face significant limitations or additional costs because of their disability would no longer qualify for cash support.

“There is no perfect system of disability support, but one that better reflects the fact that people often have multiple and fluctuating conditions must target greater support and engagement where it’s needed, and avoid waste where it’s not.”

A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “Pip is awarded based on a functional assessment that determines how a condition impacts a person’s day-to-day needs. But as the Timms Review report made clear, Pip is no longer fit for purpose and the recommendations from its final report will lay the foundation for sustainable reform.”

articles.title: DSWD demos water filtration kits to push Marcos’ bucket wisdom
articles.summary: Government officials try out filtered water after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. tells Filipinos to buy pails that they can use with water filtration kits

blocks.text: Government officials try out filtered water after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. tells Filipinos to buy pails that they can use with water filtration kits
Communities vulnerable to El Niño may soon receive water filtration kits from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).
Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian conducted on Wednesday, October 14, a live demonstration of how to use the kits, which may come in handy during water shortages.
For good measure, Gatchalian and Presidential Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro drank the filtered water in front of reporters.
The DSWD chief drank the filtered water thrice, even adding more soil to the water being filtered. Castro drank it twice.
Their live demo comes on the heels of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s advice to buy pails to collect rainwater.
Marcos said on Sunday, October 11: “Bumili na kayo ng balde para ‘pag umulan, makolekta na ninyo lahat (Buy pails so when it rains, you can collect rainwater).”

“We’ll give you the filter. We’ll teach you how to do everything so you won’t get sick and you can do the water filtration properly. And it will be healthy even for little children,” added the President in a mix of English and Filipino.
The “balde” advice drew criticism, with groups such as the August Twenty-One Movement saying it is not a real solution to the looming crisis.

On Tuesday, October 13, Castro fired back at what she called “obstructionists,” saying that the President’s remarks were serious and part of the government’s efforts to mitigate the effects of El Niño.

And, on Wednesday, Castro told Palace journalists during Gatchalian’s demo: “Alam ‘nyo, you should try [it] kasi ‘pag dumating talaga na kailangan ‘nyo ‘yan…‘di ba?” (You know, you should try drinking the filtered water because the time may come that you might need it, right?)
Reporters eventually tried the filtered water for themselves.

blocks.caption: DSWD demos water filtration kits to push Marcos’ bucket wisdom

blocks.text: Gatchalian said the DSWD will start to distribute the portable water filtration kits next week.
First in line will be local government units that have declared a state of calamity due to El Niño, as well as high-density areas in Metro Manila experiencing low water pressure.
“We’ll ask them to bring their pails and we’ll install the kits. It’s easy to install. Do they need a special pail? No,” the social welfare chief said in Filipino.
Actually, since 2024, the DSWD has been deploying buckets or jerry cans with built-in water filtration technology to disaster-hit areas without access to potable water.
Citing no actual figures, Gatchalian said many jerry cans are still in the DSWD’s stockpiles, and the agency could procure more through its quick response funds.
With the El Niño phenomenon, the DSWD is also looking into distributing the water filtration kits to families and teach them how to install the technology themselves.

All they need to do is drill a hole near the bottom of the bucket, screw on the connector, hose, and filter. All of the materials needed, including a cleaning plunger and instruction materials, are part of the DSWD kit. The filter can last for a minimum of five years with proper care and maintenance.
Each water filtration kit costs around $35 (about P2,200), according to the international non-government organization Waves for Water, which manufactured the filters for the DSWD.
For this year’s annual procurement plan, the DSWD allocated P26.9 million for 10,500 family water filtration kits sourced through its quick response funds in the 2026 national budget.

Gatchalian said the Department of Health has certified the water filtration kit as a “medical device” and vouched for the safety of the treated water. According to the DSWD, the water filtration system has 0.1 micron filters that can remove cholera, salmonella, E. Coli, and coliform bacteria.
Water sources could be deep wells, springs, rainwater, and water being rationed, according to Gatchalian.

He said the DSWD will also roll out community water depots, which are big rain catchers with a filter system and multiple faucets. The DSWD chief said these are more scalable, especially in communities with open areas and possibly, even schools.

Gatchalian said other DSWD initiatives for El Niño include the cash-for-work program for small water impounding projects and community gardens. They are also deploying air-to-water or atmospheric water machines to far-flung areas.

Castro said other government measures to boost water supply in Metro Manila are cloud seeding, better dam management, building water treatment plants, using water tankers, and activating 61 decommissioned deep wells.

All sound good, but for poor and large Filipino households that may need to store liters and liters of water, heeding the President’s advice will require them to buy multiple buckets, if not drums, to survive what is anticipated to be terribly warm and dry months ahead. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Lawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himself
articles.summary:
Account by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seat

Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his…

blocks.text: Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York City said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.

The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.

The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.

“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”
New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.

The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.

A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.

Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.

Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.

DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.

Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and now has impaired hearing.
The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says
articles.summary: Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud

blocks.text: Federal authorities investigating the Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.

The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington DC home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election.

The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.

On Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also looking into issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.

The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests, which will determine control of the House and the Senate, was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the the representative for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”.
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
after newsletter promotion

Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.

articles.title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
articles.summary: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.

blocks.text: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.
"I really like it here."

articles.title: UK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of work
articles.summary:
Restaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed scheme

Bars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young…

blocks.text: Bars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years in an effort to give them a first step on the ladder into work.

The move comes before the publication of a report on Neets by the former health secretary Alan Milburn, who has warned that the number of young people not in work or education in the UK could rise to 1.25 million over the next five years unless ministers intervene.
His full review into Britain’s crisis in youth unemployment, including recommendations to the government about how to tackle the crisis, is expected soon after the autumn budget on 28 October.

Working with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), hospitality businesses including the restaurant chains Wagamama, Nando’s and Burger King, the hotel chain Premier Inn and pub chains including Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers will offer Neets aged 18 to 24 placements of up to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.

The initiative, which will be launched by Andy Burnham during a visit to a hospitality venue on Thursday, comes after the DWP announced a similar scheme for retailers including Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and the John Lewis Partnership last month.

The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the scheme would help young people “get their first step on the ladder” and build their careers. “With the UK employment rate now the second highest in the G7, this will unlock 100,000 jobs and connect young people with employers ready to take them on and help them build a brighter future,” he said.

Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is expected to announce a review of school exclusion changes, after research showed that students who are persistently absent from school are nearly four times more likely to end up unemployed and not in education or training.
A consultation will gather views on measures to support students at risk of exclusion, improve integration into the classroom and help children stay engaged in the classroom.

Powell said: “Absence and exclusion are too often a path to disengagement, with increased risks of becoming Neet. Too many young people who fall out of education risk being permanently left on the sidelines of work and opportunity.”

Milburn has signalled that Britain’s benefits system should be overhauled, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships. Ministers are understood to be considering sweeping changes to the welfare system, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
Milburn has previously argued that a national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work.

The chancellor, John Healey, has indicated a readiness to curtail the government’s rising benefits bill, while McFadden has said there is a moral and economic case to shake up the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made demands for cuts to welfare a central plank of her attacks on the government, telling Burnham in prime minister’s questions (PMQs) on Wednesday that he should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.

But ministers will be wary of going head to head with Labour MPs, and will hope to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.

articles.title: Ex-Marineland beluga that died in Spain developed 'complex clinical condition,' aquarium says
articles.summary: A beluga whale and dolphin that died within weeks of being transferred out of Marineland had been experiencing a list of health complications and organ abnormalities that could've developed prior to…

image.caption: Photos shared on Oceanogràfic València's social media of beluga whales Cleopatra and Jelly Bean, left, and Black Sea bottlenose dolphin Echo, right. (Oceanogràfic València/Instagram)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

A beluga whale and dolphin that died within weeks of being transferred out of Marineland had been experiencing a list of health complications and organ abnormalities that could've developed prior to the transfer, Oceanogràfic València said in a news release on Oct. 14.
Oceanogràfic València says investigation continues into deaths of rescued beluga and dolphin
The Spanish aquarium said the abnormalities "may have developed before the animals arrived in Valencia" and may have not been apparent in health assessments before its transfer.

Beluga Jelly Bean and dolphin Echo arrived, along with three other dolphins and beluga whale Cleopatra, to the aquarium in Valencia, Spain, on Aug. 27, but died just under a month after the move. Meanwhile, four other Marineland whales — Peekachu, Rain, Osiris and Caspian — have died since the rescue at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, along with another beluga that did not come from Marineland.
The necropsy was performed by Oceanogràfic València, which shared an English translation of a news release with their preliminary findings with CBC News.
Per the preliminary findings, Jelly Bean developed "a complex clinical condition," showing signs of metabolic disorder and electrolyte imbalance in the days before her death.

items: Ex-Marineland beluga whale dies in Chicago aquarium
Marineland belugas that died in Chicago had chronic inflammatory disease, preliminary necropsy findings show
Marineland dolphin dies at Spain aquarium, marking 5th death after rescue transfer

blocks.text: Abnormalities were found in Jelly Bean's heart, as well as an enlarged thyroid gland and shrunken adrenal glands, all organs responsible for regulating metabolism, according to the post-mortem findings.

During her final days, the aquarium said she'd been exhibiting unusual behaviour, ingesting water which "further complicated her condition." They said the 19-year-old beluga whale had experienced "feeding difficulties" upon arrival, but she'd been showing signs of improvement.
She died on Sept. 18.
CBC News reached out to Marineland for comment on the necropsy's preliminary findings, but did not hear back in time for publication.
Dolphin needed 'continuous veterinary care'
Echo, a 30-year-old Black Sea bottlenose dolphin, was fifth among the six animals that died in the first month since the transfer.

According to Oceanogràfic València's news release, she arrived with a "severe vision impairment and limited mobility in one of her flippers." And in the days leading up to her death, they say Echo was showing neurological and respiratory symptoms, which required "continuous veterinary care."
They say she had "inflammation in the brain and nervous tissue, consistent with toxoplasmosis."
The Spanish aquarium says it has specialists investigating "the responsible infectious agent" and that direct transmission between dolphins of the parasitic disease does not happen.
Investigation ongoing
Oceanogràfic València says it will continue to investigate the deaths of Jelly Bean and Echo.
The aquarium is working with pathologists specialists from CEU Cardenal Herrera University and Valencia's Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, and veterinary medicine research groups.

"This was a rescue mission, aimed at giving the remaining belugas the best chance at a safe, healthy life based on individual health assessments, with an understanding of the risks involved," a spokesperson for Fisheries and Oceans Canada told CBC News in an email Wednesday.

"Some of these whales carried long-term health issues from their time at Marineland, and those often don't show until it's too late," the spokesperson said. "We remain thankful to the experienced professionals involved in this operation, including the team in Spain who cared for Jelly Bean."
Marine mammal scientist expects more deaths

Animal Welfare Institute marine mammal scientist Naomi Rose acknowledges the feat to rescue the captive animals, but she finds it disingenuous for the aquariums to claim that the animals' pre-existing conditions were not "clinically apparent."
"We all knew the whales at Marineland were sick," Rose told CBC News on Wednesday.
Why Marineland's last living belugas are on 'death watch'
She said the stress of transport can linger for up to a year and potentially cause an extreme reaction like death.
"We could be seeing deaths for the next months. This isn't over."
Oceanogràfic València says its veterinary and animal care staff will closely monitor the remaining beluga whale Cleopatra and three other dolphins, who are "progressing well."

Beluga whales Balor and Zephyr, relocated to Georgia Aquarium, are "integrating well" with other whales and "adjusting to their new habitat," according to an aquarium Instagram post last month. But the Atlanta-based aquarium did note Zephyr's decreased appetite sand said Balor "has not gained weight as steadily as expected."
SeaWorld told CBC News on Sept. 17 that the 16 other beluga whales they took — 13 of which have been relocated to the San Antonio, Texas, and three to San Diego — "continue to be in stable health."

items: 4 Marineland belugas, 1 dolphin, died after being transferred. Why the rest remain on 'death watch'
