articles.title: Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
articles.summary: Serhii Kuznietsov is accused of attacking civilian infrastructure in the 2022 sabotage of the Russian gas pipeline to Germany. His lawyers called Nord Stream a military target, and said their client…

image.caption: Serhii Kuznietsov's defense team argued that the alleged actions should not be deemed a criminal actImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The trial of a former Ukrainian special forces officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, opened in the northern German city of Hamburg on Wednesday amid considerable public and press interest.

Kuznietsov is accused of leading the September 2022 sabotage operation that put the undersea Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines linking Russian to Germany out of action. The pipelines remain inactive four years later, with no sign of plans to ever reactivate them as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine heads into its fifth winter.

Prosecutors accuse the Ukrainian of participation in a war crime by targeting civilian infrastructure, but his defense lawyers on Wednesday argued that the case should be dismissed entirely on multiple grounds.

blocks.caption: The defense lawyers argue that the case should be thrown out entirely, saying their client is forbidden from speaking with them or anybody else about the caseImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Kuznietsov's lawyers say on opening day?
A team of three lawyers representing Kuznietsov questioned the premise of the trial in court.
One of Kuznietsov's lawyers, Nicola Canestrini, argued that it was not valid to try the officer on war crimes charges for an attack on civilian infrastructure.

He argued that the pipeline, which provided half of Germany's natural gas imports prior to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, was ultimately a "Russian weapon," given the importance of energy revenues for funding Moscow's military.
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked the court.
After the charges were read out, the judge asked Kuznietsov if he wanted to comment, and he said that he did not.
His lawyers argue that this silence extends beyond not speaking in court and say this should be the main grounds for dismissal.
They say Kuznietsov is sworn to secrecy by his home government in Ukraine and so is unable to discuss his case or potential exonerating evidence with anyone, including his legal representatives.

"He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers," defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court. In German law, Meyer-Lohkamp argued: "Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted."

blocks.caption: A small group of demonstrators stood outside the court on Wednesday arguing that the wrong party to the war in Ukraine was on trialImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What was the mood in court in Hamburg?
DW's Matthew Moore was on hand in the court in northern Germany on Wednesday.
There is huge interest in this court case, Moore reported. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told Moore they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.

"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.

blocks.caption: Based on investigative reporting and a Bojan Pancevski book on the sabotage published this year, Kuznietsov coordinated a small and unlikely team made up not of professional spies or soldiers, but rather people with relevant specialist skills like deep-sea divers and explosives expertsImage: Mark…

blocks.text: Geramny's Wadephul: 'We will deal with any outcome'
The case has been highly politically awkward for Germany — a staunch supporter of Ukraine despite investigators pursuing a trail that led to Kuznietsov and other suspects.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly denied any Ukrainian involvement in the operation, and had also resisted Kuznietsov's extradition to Germany after his arrest in Italy last year, arguing that there was no case to answer.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul declined to comment on the trial on Wednesday, saying that the most important thing for now was for the case to proceed with no political interference or restrictions.
"We will deal with any outcome, and we will, of course, take it into account in our political calculations," he told a press conference in Berlin.
Court dates for the trial are currently scheduled through February of next year but this could be subject to change in either direction.
With additional reporting from DW's Matthew Moore in Hamburg.

articles.title: How Trump’s diesel deal with Russia will impact the United States and Ukraine
articles.summary: US President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia has alarmed Ukraine and its allies. What is he hoping to achieve at home, and what does the deal mean for Kyiv and Moscow?

image.caption: Donald Trump now allows Russian diesel imports into the USImage: Eric Lee/REUTERS

blocks.text: Many Ukrainians and Europeans viewed news from Washington over the past weekend as a stab in the back by their US ally. First, President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which involves a temporary easing of US sanctions against Moscow.

And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same.
'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine'

Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine."
He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia.

All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory.
"The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD.
The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day.
"The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said.
Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them.
'No concrete military benefits for Russia'
The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia.
He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.

"Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said.

Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
European alternatives to US intelligence

A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact.
While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems.

As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran.
Support for Ukraine across both US parties

Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia, known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor, who has since died.

Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.

blocks.caption: There is broad bipartisan support for Ukraine in US CongressImage: Valerio Rosati/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW.

He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia."

Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian

articles.title: Mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
articles.summary: An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award. See a selection of the other…

blocks.text: Science·Photos

An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award. See a selection of the other winning photos here.
Youth award goes to photo of hard-working dung beetle
(Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Federico Veronesi captured "The Aftermath" while tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley in Namibia. He noticed unusual drag marks in the sand of the dry riverbed. When he caught up to a family of elephants, he saw an adult female with a calf's leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
Kathy Moran, chair of the jury for the 2026 competition, described the photo as working on "so many levels."
"Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it's proof that animals have cognition," she wrote in a news release announcing the winners.
In addition to winning the grand prize, the photo also won the Behaviour: Mammals category.

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the U.K.-based Natural History Museum in London, with a stated goal to share nature's stories and insights about environmental challenges that need our attention.
This year, the annual competition — the 62nd edition — attracted 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.
It awards top prizes to both an adult photographer and a young photographer under 18.
This year's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year prize was won by Oscar Whitfield, a young British photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and frequently returns there during school holidays.
His photo, captured while lying on the ground, shows a close-up of a dung beetle hard at work pushing a ball of dung. It was also the winner in the 11 to 14 years age bracket.
(Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the year)

Officially, there were no Canadian category winners this year. However, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, who lives in Germany and won this year's Rising Star Award, is a Canadian citizen who has previously told CBC News his parents were both born in Canada, and he has relatives in Ottawa and Nova Scotia.

His featured photo, "Afternoon snack," is a close-up of a robber fly preying on a flesh fly. "The bubbles forming in the victim's eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked out," the photo's description reads.
(Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
Canadians can see the 100-photo exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto from Nov 7, 2026, to Feb 28, 2027.
It opens at the Natural History Museum in London this Friday.
Here are some of the other category winners.
Amelie Davis, of the U.K., won the 10 years and under bracket with this photo of a common carder bee in southern England, captured with her father's smartphone.
(Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A California newt lays eggs while clasping vegetation that already contains another newt's egg clutch in the winner of the Amphibians and Reptiles category, captured by U.S. photographer Anton Sorokin. The newt will stay like this until the egg mass swells to a size too large to be eaten by a predator.
(Anton Sorokin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Greek photographer Agorastos Papatsanis used UV light to make these fluorescent bonnet mushrooms glow brightly on a decaying log on the lower slopes of Greece's Mount Olympus. The image won the Plants and Fungi category.
(Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A young bull elephant sprays water on a group of zebras at a waterhole in the Chyulu Hills of Kenya in this photo, the winner of the Animals in their Environment category, captured by James Lewin using a camera converted to infrared to soften harsh lighting.
(James Lewin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

articles.title: Japanese journalist arrest in Russia's Far East draws rebuke from Tokyo in latest diplomatic spat with Moscow
articles.summary: A journalist for a Japanese newspaper was arrested on suspicion of spying in Russia's Far East. A geopolitical rivalry over disputed islands in the region has recently caused tension.

image.caption: A journalist for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was arrested by Russia's FSBImage: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Russia's ambassador after a Japanese journalist was arrested by Russia's FSB security agency on suspicion of espionage.
What do know so far?

The journalist's arrest comes amid a dispute in a dispute between Russia and Japan over the four southernmost islands of the Kuril Island chain, which are controlled by Moscow and claimed by Tokyo. The archipelago in the northwest Pacific is near the Russian island of Sakhalin where the man was arrested.

Russia's Federal Security Service announced the arrest on Tuesday and claimed the journalist, who works for the northern Japanese Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was gathering information about Russian defense capability on behalf of Japanese intelligence.

In a statement, Japan's Foreign Ministry lodged a "strong protest" against Russia for "detaining this Japanese national and issuing unilateral statements regarding the matter, while the Japanese government has not received any explanation concerning the detained national as yet."

On Wednesday, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Tokyo called for Russia to treat the detainee fairly and humanely, while asking Russian authorities for more information about his arrest.
Kihara added that Japanese officials have been unable to contact the man, his condition is unknown, and Moscow had not responded to Tokyo's requests for access.
"We'll do everything we can for the protection of the Japanese citizen," he said.
Russia claims Japan using journalists as spies

Russian authorities identified the journalist as Yuki Imai. The Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper has not yet confirmed the journalist's identity, saying it is still gathering details of what could have led to the arrest.
The newspaper said the man had been reporting in Russia on a journalist visa and was supposed to leave on Monday.

In footage on Russian state television, a man is seen being placed in handcuffs by three masked men in black uniforms, and then being accompanied by FSB agents onto a plane. The man is then seen in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for two months.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova claimed that Japan is using accredited journalists in Russia to gather sensitive security information.

Kimitake Nakamura, head of the European Affairs Bureau at Japan's Foreign Ministry, said he has asked Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to quickly arrange a meeting between the detained journalist and the Japanese government.
Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands
Japan-Russia Kuril Islands dispute

The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.
Bilateral tensions were aggravated by Japan joining Western sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

The dispute reignited in August after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the Kurils for the first time, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling the visit "absolutely unacceptable." Putin was only the second Russian leader to ever visit the islands
Russia has also increased its military presence on the islands in recent years, including by deploying missile systems, expanding air fields, and using the islands for live fire drills.
In Wednesday's Foreign Ministry statement, Nakamura reiterated Japan's territorial claims over the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which Tokyo calls the "Northern Territory."

articles.title: Student protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with police
articles.summary:
Government building and two banks set on fire as tens of thousands take to streets over education costs and corruption

Tens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the…
articles.byline: Guardian staff and agencies in Tirana

blocks.text: Tens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and ⁠corruption.

Police responded with water ⁠cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.

The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, ⁠the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced ​growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top ‌officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures ‌as unpalatable alternatives.

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with police in central Tirana. Photograph: Adnan Beci/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development ‌of a luxury resort along Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.
“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.
Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.
Student ‌organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.

The unrest is part of a ​broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.
Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.
The government ⁠condemned the violence.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A government building and two banks were set on fire during the protests. Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters

blocks.text: Albana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used ​as an excuse for violence, city ​destruction or ugly fighting in the middle ​of the road. I call on ​students and every ‌honest citizen who believes in ​the right to ​protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”

The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.
Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.
A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,”
Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.

articles.title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
articles.summary: The Irish writer is best known for novels such as Normal People, Intermezzo and Conversations With Friends.

blocks.text: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.

In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK.
"I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said.
Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies.
Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves.
Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.
Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.
Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.
Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work.
"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format."
Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories."
The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage.
The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza.
In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK.
"The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."

In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested.
On Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence.
"After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK."
Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced".
Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action".
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action.
About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month.

articles.title: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
articles.summary:
Global human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activity

The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling…

blocks.text: The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.

The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.

The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.

The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.
Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.
The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.
A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.
The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.

The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.

The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.
after newsletter promotion

The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.

A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.

The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.

Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.
Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

articles.title: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff in steepest cuts since 2022
articles.summary: The cuts equate to around 6% of the streaming giant's total workforce worldwide.

blocks.text: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".

The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.

In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.

Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

articles.title: 3rd member of Canadian Armed Forces charged in kidnapping probe: Toronto police
articles.summary: A third member of the Canadian Armed Forces, and four other people, were arrested and charged in a kidnapping probe that led to the arrest of two other members of Canada’s military reserves, Toronto…

image.caption: Police recovered at least four firearms, 2,700 rounds of ammunition and large quantities of cocaine, methamphetamine and other controlled substances during the investigation. (Keira Mahoney/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

A third member of the Canadian Armed Forces, and four other people, were arrested and charged in a kidnapping probe that led to the arrest of two other members of Canada’s military reserves, Toronto police announced Wednesday.
2 other military reserve members, 4 civilians also arrested and charged, police say

Joe Matthews, chief superintendent with Toronto Police Services, said the accused were arrested following an investigation that started while looking into a kidnapping on July 25. Police allege the victim was confined in the car at gunpoint, handcuffed and was assaulted as suspects tried to access cryptocurrency assets.

items: 2 Canadian Armed Forces members arrested in organized crime, kidnapping probe, DND says

blocks.text: Jack Miley, a 24-year-old from Toronto and reserve member of the CAF, was arrested on Sept. 24 and is facing seven charges including kidnapping for ransom with a firearm, forcible confinement and a number of firearm charges, said Matthews.

Earlier this month, police announced Talarambage Fernando and James Moreau, both reserve members of the 7 Toronto Regiment, were arrested on Aug. 11 in relation to the same investigation. Miley is a member of a different regiment, police said Wednesday.
Four civilians were also arrested, police said.

Police recovered at least four firearms during the investigation and 2,700 rounds of ammunition, about half of them blanks, were allegedly stolen from the military. They also found large quantities of cocaine, methamphetamine and other controlled substances.

Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, are facing a combined total of 49 charges, police said following their arrest. The pair have since been removed from their duties and their access to military facilities and bases has been restricted, according to the Department of National Defence.

Both have been charged with kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement, unauthorized possession of a firearm in a motor vehicle, use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence, and mischief interfere with property.

Matthews said it’s not clear how the seven accused all knew each other, but said that’s part of the ongoing investigation. He said there’s nothing to indicate the accused are tied to any larger organized crime circles.

International grouping of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship

The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of…

blocks.text: The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.

Wednesday’s audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.

“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.

It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, Ipac, which counts members from all the UK’s major parties, says.

In an endorsement, the former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
While the report accepts that “disengagement was not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies, and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
It identifies emerging technologies such as AI as posing new challenges, in terms of disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.

“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The Guardian has contacted the UK government and the Chinese embassy in London for comment.

It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.

“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom;, you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

articles.title: Turkey: Government raids, takes over top news channel
articles.summary: Turkish authorities have raided the Istanbul offices of Halk TV, halting broadcasts, appointing a trustee and opening an investigation. It is the latest chapter of a decadeslong media capture by…

image.caption: Authorities raided Halk TV and cut from live news to a Turkish film classic from 1973Image: ANKA

blocks.text: Turkish authorities took control of Halk TV on Wednesday — raiding the outlet's Istanbul studios, cutting all broadcasts and appointing a government trustee to oversee the company during an investigation into alleged corruption.

"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee [manager] has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," posted the popular news channel on X as police guarded the building, financial crimes agents searched offices and computers, and technicians cut live news channel feeds and YouTube broadcasts.
Footage posted online showed the moment the channel's live broadcast feed was cut — during an interview about a huge investment-fund scandal — and replaced with a classic Turkish film from 1973.

blocks.caption: Police surrounded Halk TV's Istanbul studio early Wednesday morningImage: ANKA

blocks.text: In a statement, the Istanbul Prosecutor's Office announced that Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroglu is under investigation for "bribery, tender-rigging, ‌and laundering of assets derived ⁠from ⁠crime."
Government trustees were installed at Halk TV and other companies owned by Mahiroglu.
In all, prosecutors say 17 detention warrants were issued, with 11 individuals taken into custody.

Mahiroglu, who lives abroad and is being sought by authorities, decried what he called "a dark day for Turkey" and blasted the allegations against him as "baseless" in a video posted on X. The pro-opposition broadcaster said seven of his relatives had been detained by authorities.
"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," he said. "Using the judiciary as a weapon is the greatest harm inflicted on Turkey."
German gov't 'deeply concerned' about DW journalist's arrest
Erdogan smothering all press dissent in Turkey
Press freedom groups and opposition parties joined Mahiroglu in condemning the government takeover as the latest step by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to silence his critics.
Ozgur Ozel, leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid was an abuse of government power.

Ozel called the raids "weak and cowardly," saying it was no coincidence they occurred just as jailed Erdogan opponent, Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was set to make headlines delivering his defense in a sprawling graft trial.
"Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit," Ozel wrote on X. "Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country."
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.
In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Istanbul's suspended mayor Imamoglu on trial
Similar pattern as Erdogan government eats up one media outlet after another

Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against Halk TV, stating: "The appointment of a trustee at Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression. This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public's right to access information, is unacceptable."
Halk TV's takeover made it the fifth major Turkish news outlet forcefully put under trusteeship, ​following similar situations at Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Veysel Ok, co-director of media-rights watchdog MLSA, said the intervention against Halk TV was "one of the most significant steps in the government's efforts to monopolize the flow of information."

"Halk TV's position as the most-watched news channel also reveals the real target of this intervention: Depriving the public of its right to access news from different sources," Ok told French news agency AFP.
"Defending press freedom means defending the public's right to learn the truth, hold the government to account and freely decide its own future."

The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X, saying the government was clearly "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was instead "aiming for the 100%."
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."

articles.title: Hunger rises to 22.6% in Q3 – SWS
articles.summary: More Filipinos experienced involuntary hunger in the third quarter of the year, according to a Social Weather Stations survey.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
Results of the Sept. 21 to 27 survey released Wednesday showed that 22.6 percent of respondents experienced being hungry and having nothing to eat at least once in the past three months.
KJ Rosales
MANILA, Philippines — More Filipinos experienced involuntary hunger in the third quarter of the year, according to a Social Weather Stations survey.
It went up slightly from 20.3 percent in June, but still below the 23.2 percent in March.
The latest hunger rate comprises 16.2 percent of respondents who said their families experienced moderate hunger (from 15.8 percent) and 6.4 percent who experienced severe hunger (from 4.5 percent).
Moderate hunger is experienced “only once” or “a few times” in the last three months, while severe hunger is “often” or “always” in the last three months.

Across areas, the September hunger rate was highest among respondents in Metro Manila at 27 percent (from 21 percent), followed by those in Mindanao at 23.7 percent (from 24 percent), rest of Luzon at 23.6 percent (from 17.3 percent) and the Visayas at 16 percent (from 22.3 percent).

Involuntary hunger increased among poor households, from 24.5 percent to 27.9 percent and from 29.9 percent, while it was steady among not poor or borderline poor respondents, from 16.1 percent to 16.2 percent.

articles.title: COA flags Sandiganbayan justices’ foreign trips
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan was called out for failing to justify with proper documentation its expenses related to overseas trips of its justices and personnel, as well as organizing events in four-star and…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
The photo of the Commission on Audit's office in Quezon City.
The STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan was called out for failing to justify with proper documentation its expenses related to overseas trips of its justices and personnel, as well as organizing events in four-star and five-star venues across the country.

In its annual audit report for the anti-graft court in 2025 published on its website yesterday, the Commission on Audit (COA) reported the “granting and liquidation of CAs (cash advances) for official foreign travels of SB officials and employees for CY (calendar year) 2025, totaling P11,869,847.98, were not fully supported with complete documentary requirements.”

The amount was disbursed for seven foreign trips – mostly conferences and training – to the US state of Missouri; Victoria, Australia; Budapest, Hungary; Dubai, United Arab Emirates; Doha in Qatar and Singapore from September to December 2025, according to the COA report.
It noted that the costliest trips were the ones in Hungary at over P2.5 million, Dubai at over P1.88 million and Singapore at over P1.82 million.

“Review of the above-listed CAs revealed that the documentary requirements for granting the said CAs such as: (a) letters of invitation; (b) plane fare quotations and (c) flight itineraries were not submitted,” the COA noted.
From the total amount of over P11.8 million, over P7.1 million lacked narrative reports.

Meanwhile, the cost of roundtrip tickets to Hungary worth P621,783 for the attendance of “three justices” to “a special course” on artificial intelligence in criminal legal profession “could not be determined if within the allowable rates prescribed for foreign travels of officials” under relevant policies of the Sandiganbayan.

According to the anti-graft court’s rules cited by COA, only the presiding justice is entitled to “full business class” while the rest of its workforce should take only “official economy class” in case flights would not be subsidized by the host country or sponsoring organization.

The state auditor also flagged the Sandiganbayan’s “lease of privately-owned venues for various official activities,” which was “not consistently supported with the required justifications and documentary evidence.”

The anti-graft court “entered into 12 contracts with private lessors under negotiated procurement,” wherein a total of P13,649,836.40 was spent to use “mostly five-star and four-star hotels… within and outside Metro Manila” for its various events that included seminars, workshops and its Christmas party in 2025.

Most of the funds were disbursed for the anti-graft court’s “executive briefing and capacity building” held at the heritage-themed Las Casas Filipinas de Acuzar resort in Bagac, Bataan with a bill of P5,175,200.

Other activities – including a tree-planting that was included in a special en banc session – were held at five-star hotels, namely Clark Marriott Hotel in Pampanga and Baguio Country Club, and at four-star Seda Vertis North hotel in Quezon City.

“Further examination of DVs (disbursement vouchers) and supporting records disclosed that several transactions were processed without submission of required documents necessary to demonstrate prior consideration of available government-owned venues, written justification establishing that the lease of privately-owned venues was more economical and efficient, or justification supporting the use of four- or five-star hotels,” the COA said.

articles.title: NBI tags 10 persons of interest in Laos drug haul
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation has identified 10 persons and entities of interest in the seizure of 512 kilograms of suspected shabu in Laos, which authorities believe was intended for shipment…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
The NBI vowed to pursue everyone responsible for or involved in the alleged attempt to smuggle the drugs worth P3.5 billion into the country.
PNA / File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has identified 10 persons and entities of interest in the seizure of 512 kilograms of suspected shabu in Laos, which authorities believe was intended for shipment to the Philippines.
The shipment, which was reportedly bound for the Philippines on a private jet, was intercepted on Oct. 1 by Laotian authorities.
The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) has identified two Filipinos allegedly involved in the plan to transport the drugs.
One of them, identified as Dibaroson Fahad from Marawi, has been arrested and is being investigated for alleged links to a Davao-based drug syndicate.

The other suspect, identified only as Boyet, allegedly chartered the aircraft and paid for it through a bank transfer. However, the PDEA said he left the country for Hong Kong a day before the operation.
At a press briefing on Monday, PDEA chief Isagani Nerez said traffickers may have shifted to air transport after repeated maritime interdictions disrupted their operations.
The drugs were believed to be intended for Metro Manila.
BOC gathers information
Meanwhile, Bureau of Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said the BOC has gathered information about the shabu shipment.

At yesterday’s Kapihan sa Manila Bay news forum, Nepomuceno said he received information on reported attempts to bring illegal drugs into the country, but would leave it to the PDEA to disclose the information.
“To be honest, I have some information already and details but I would respect PDEA in handling it. By law, PDEA is the primary agency. I do not want to preempt,” said Nepomuceno.
He said someone shared information on “who they talked to, who hired the airplanes and how many times this happened. We already have the information,” he added.

Nepomuceno said based on the information gathered by intelligence officers, it has happened before and the drug suspects allegedly used private planes to transport the contraband and that their planes landed in “private hangars of private companies.”
“We would be looking into that,” he added.
The BOC will review the current setup with hangars for private planes, some catering to “VVIP” (very, very important persons) that may include businessmen and politicians.
He said while the BOC has personnel assigned to these private hangars, they might have been intimidated by the presence of VVIPs.

“So, I will see how we could strengthen the BOC’s capability with these private companies. I just hope that our VVIPs, from the business sector and political sector, would not get mad. I hope that when we fix the entry and exits for private hangars, they would not take it out on our people,” Nepomuceno said.

He added, “Let us admit that these areas are sensitive because this is where the super VVIPs pass through. We cannot just impose our own rules. We would respect the sensibilities and sensitivities of these private entrances and exits. But we would have to do our job.” – Evelyn Macarian

articles.title: VP Sara told: Stop playing victim
articles.summary: As her legal team prepares to take its turn in presenting her side in the impeachment trial, Vice President Sara Duterte should focus on building up her defense instead of portraying herself as a…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As her legal team prepares to take its turn in presenting her side in the impeachment trial, Vice President Sara Duterte should focus on building up her defense instead of portraying herself as a victim, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said yesterday.
“They always play the victim card. So again, let us remove that ‘kawawa naman ang VP syndrome’,” Kapunan said.
“She is not the victim, the public is the victim here. You’re talking about public funds. You’re talking about a public officer and impeachment,” she said.

“She should start presenting or building up her case. She should start talking to her father so that she is able to explain the accounts of the father and herself. She should start talking to her husband,” she said, referring to detained former president Rodrigo Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio.

The veteran lawyer argued that attention should focus on the hundreds of millions in the bank accounts and assets of Duterte and her family. “Whose money is this? These are public funds,” she pointed out.
Malacañang said it’s not questioning the move of the prosecution.

“Well, everybody, we are all for the truth. We are all for transparency and accountability. But if it’s the legal strategy of the prosecution, we cannot question whatever decision they make,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
Castro believes the evidence and documents presented relating to the withdrawn articles would likely to stay in the minds of Filipinos, although the Vice President can address them in various ways.
Citing records, prosecution witness accountant-lawyer Alexander Cabrera earlier confirmed the existence of P817.87 million in unexplained wealth of Duterte and her spouse.
He emphasized his figure was conservative, as the amount could reach P1.5 billion between 2022 and 2025 if other documents were included in his analysis.

House of Representatives impeachment team adviser and spokesman Robert Ace Barbers, meanwhile, maintained that the prosecution’s withdrawal of three of four cases against Duterte did not deprive her of due process.

“They (defense counsels) were given the opportunity to cross-examine our witnesses. The defense was also given the chance to examine or scrutinize the documentary evidence that we all presented,” Barbers pointed out.

The prosecution has opted to proceed solely with Article II, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth, discrepancies in Duterte’s asset declarations and the alleged retention of business interests in violation of constitutional restrictions.

“They were allowed to make the necessary reply. And that is the real essence of due process. That’s why I don’t know where Senator-Judge Cayetano is coming from when he said that due process will be sacrificed here,” he said.
For retired Supreme Court associate justice Noel Tijam, the dropping of the three Articles of Impeachment would “fortify suspicion that the impeachment court is a kangaroo court.”

“With the dropping of the three Articles of Impeachment against the Vice President, the spotlight has been refocused no longer solely on the Vice President but on Congress, the ombudsman and the executive department,” Tijam wrote on Facebook.
He added that the development would also spawn perception that the impeachment court “is weak and condescending to the defense and subservient to the prosecution.”

Meanwhile, Sen. Panfilo Lacson debunked Duterte spokesman Paolo Panelo’s claim that up to P500 million in public funds had been wasted hearing two Articles of Impeachment that were later withdrawn by the prosecution.

Lacson said the Senate’s budget for the ongoing impeachment trial was sourced from the P27.5-million continuing appropriations in last year’s national budget, when the first impeachment complaint was filed and later voided by the Supreme Court.

“Where did he get his P25M/day figure? As far as I know, the GAA 2025 budget for the impeachment trial, most of which has remained unspent (only roughly P2 million was disbursed for the judges’ robes and other items) from the original P27.5 million, is now being used under the ‘continuing appropriations’ provision in the General Appropriations Act,” Lacson said.
Lacson said Panelo might be referring to the Senate’s P25-million daily operating cost. - Ghio Ong, Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Helen Flores

articles.title: Government rolls out water filters amid ‘super’ El Niño
articles.summary: The government will start distributing free portable water filtration kits to communities next week to ensure adequate supply of potable water amid a looming super El Niño, Social Welfare…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The government will start distributing free portable water filtration kits to communities next week to ensure adequate supply of potable water amid a looming super El Niño, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian announced yesterday.
At a Palace briefing, Gatchalian and officials of the Department of Social Welfare and Development demonstrated the use of the filtration kits, which are intended for household and community use.
Gatchalian said the government has a stockpile of the Sawyer water filtration system with bucket adapter kits supplied by international nongovernment organization Waves for Water.
The system is certified by the Department of Health as a medical device and has passed the Philippine National Standards for Drinking Water.
It uses 0.1-micron filters that can remove bacteria associated with cholera, salmonella, E. coli and coliform contamination from deep wells, springs and rainwater.
The DSWD will launch the filtration system in Tondo, Manila next week, prioritizing areas under a state of calamity and densely populated communities in Metro Manila.

Larger filtration systems equipped with rain catchers and faucets are also being deployed and operated as community drinking water stations in San Felipe, Zambales and Mayantoc, Tarlac, while similar facilities have been used in Batanes.
Other government agencies are also stepping up efforts to mitigate the effects of El Niño.

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), for its part, is promoting nature-based solutions to help farms withstand drought, including bamboo plantations to retain soil moisture, soil conservation structures to prevent erosion and small water impounding systems to provide alternative water supplies.
The department is also working with irrigation agencies and local communities to improve water management and promote sustainable farming practices.

The Philippine National Police (PNP), meanwhile, has ordered police camps, stations and regional headquarters to adopt “water-smart” protocols, conserve water, install rainwater harvesting systems and repair leaking infrastructure.
A fast lane for legally imported agricultural products is also being considered by the Bureau of Customs (BOC) to speed up the release of food supplies and help prevent shortages amid El Niño.

“We have to double the facilitation of imported food items especially during El Niño, if there would be a shortage in rice and vegetables,” BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said at a forum yesterday.
He added that the agency would explore the proposal and support the Department of Agriculture (DA)’s programs, provided importers have complete permits and comply with requirements.
P6.5 billion losses
Barely a month since the super El Niño started, agricultural losses from the El Niño have reached more than P6.539 billion, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.
Citing DA data, the NDRRMC said the losses cover about 159,211 metric tons of totally and partially damaged crops.

Cagayan Valley recorded the biggest share with more than P4.967 billion in agricultural losses, followed by the Cordillera Administrative Region with P934.9 million and the Davao Region with P410 million.
The Zamboanga Peninsula reported P95.8 million in losses, followed by Bicol with P37.4 million and Central Visayas with P22.7 million.

Other affected regions include Caraga with P22 million, Calabarzon with P19.7 million, Soccsksargen with P12.5 million, Central Luzon with more than P1.8 million and Western Visayas with over P1.8 million.
As of Tuesday, the NDRRMC reported that 215,386 farmers and fisherfolk had been affected by the dry conditions in their farms and fishing grounds.
About 451,889 people have also been affected across various provinces, while 109 cities and municipalities have been placed under a state of calamity.
In response, the government has provided more than P46.4 million in food and non-food assistance to 36,275 affected families.
Inflation
The worsening dry conditions could drive up consumer prices and weigh on economic growth, Chinabank Research warned.
In a report, the bank estimated that inflation could exceed eight percent under a severe El Niño scenario.
“We expect inflation to peak in the fourth quarter of 2026 and remain below eight percent in our baseline, although a severe El Niño could push it above that level,” Chinabank said.
The bank said reduced production of rice, corn and other crops would likely be the most immediate source of price pressures.
Higher electricity demand and constraints on water and hydropower supplies could also contribute to inflation.

“With inflation already elevated, a more severe El Niño remains a key upside risk to our inflation outlook,” the bank noted, adding that while earlier interest rate increases could help contain second-round price pressures, monetary tightening has limited ability to address inflation driven by supply disruptions. - Keisha Ta-asan, Michael Punongbayan, Josiah Antonio, Mark Ernest Villeza, Rainier Allan Ronda, Evelyn Macairan

articles.title: ‘House realigned P206 billion in 2027 national budget’
articles.summary: Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito has raised concerns over the House of Representatives’ realignments in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

blocks.text: Headlines
October 15, 2026 | 12:00am

Ejercito expressed concern over the P130-billion reduction for foreign-assisted projects (FAP), which are funded through loan agreements with partners such as the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
Philstar.com / File
MANILA, Philippines — Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito has raised concerns over the House of Representatives’ realignments in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
Ejercito noted that an estimated P206 billion was altered from the executive branch’s original spending plan and slashed funds for big-ticket infrastructure and preventive health care.
The allocation for FAPs is supposed to pay off the multibillion-peso loans from JICA and ADB that were used for big-ticket infrastructure projects including the Metro Manila Subway.
“There was noticeable slashing of funds for major programs, especially foreign-assisted programs,” Ejercito said.
“The more we delay, the bigger the problem gets. We have to finish all of these major infra so they can be put to use,” he added.
The Japanese government has sought clarifications from the Philippine government regarding delays in JICA-funded projects.

Ejercito also noted a P9.5-billion cut from the Calamity Fund amid looming threats from a strong El Niño, as well as an apparent shift toward short-term social assistance at the expense of preventive health care programs.

Under the Department of Health’s budget, the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) meant to improve hospitals was slashed by P4.5 billion, the immunization program lost P4 billion and health promotion programs were cut by P2 billion.
In contrast, allocations for the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) surged by P23.9 billion.
MAIFIP is a controversial health care program, which has been criticized as a “discretionary fund” vulnerable to political patronage.

“It’s a puzzle to me because one of the key factors of the UHC (Universal Health Care) is to strengthen the preventive side. And they slashed it. What are we doing? We remove immunization and health promotion then when people get sick we provide medical assistance?” said Ejercito, a principal author of the UHC Act.
Flood control
In the Department of Public Works and Highways, right-of-way acquisitions were reduced by P2.6 billion while flood mitigation structures within major river basins saw a P4.6-billion cut.
Meanwhile, general construction and maintenance received an additional P13 billion and overall flood mitigation items were increased by P8.04 billion.
Ejercito cautioned against over-relying on unconditional subsidies, stressing that long-term infrastructure investment generates sustained employment.
“Budget process is a balancing act,” he said.

Ejercito announced that the finance committee received the official copy of the House General Appropriations Bill on Tuesday and copies were distributed to senators and committee vice chairs to begin scrutiny.

With only limited fiscal space left for Senate institutional amendments, Ejercito said the Senate would demand Regional Development Council approvals and disallow lump-sum allocations for flood control, prioritizing only uncompleted projects along major river basins and the top 10 flood-prone areas.
The finance committee set an Oct. 23 deadline for subcommittees to submit their reports, with civil society organizations and watchdogs scheduled for consultations on Oct. 26.
Ejercito plans to sponsor the committee report on Nov. 11, open plenary debates on Nov. 23 and targets the signing of the 2027 national budget by the second week of December.

articles.title: Duterte defense wants fewer witnesses, evidence
articles.summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte is not satisfied with the prosecution’s efforts to shorten its list of evidence and witnesses in his upcoming trial for crimes against…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 12:00am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte attends the fourth status conference at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, on Oct. 13, 2026.
International Criminal Court / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte is not satisfied with the prosecution’s efforts to shorten its list of evidence and witnesses in his upcoming trial for crimes against humanitbefore the International Criminal Court (ICC).
During the fourth status conference on Tuesday, defense lawyer Peter Haynes pointed out that some of the prosecution witnesses may be “filtered out” from the list.

“They include people who haven’t made a witness statement, people who give precisely similar evidence to other witnesses. They include witnesses with whom the prosecution hasn’t had any contact for a long period of time and witnesses who explicitly said they want nothing further to do with the proceedings,” he said.
But the prosecution maintained that they have already made efforts to shorten the time needed for them to present their evidence.

Trial lawyer Edward Jeremy said the prosecution has reclassified some of its intended witnesses, including filing a request for admission of prior recorded testimony instead of calling them to testify in person.
“With our latest reclassifications, we’ve saved 20 hours of court time. The 193 (hours) figure is now down to 173. We will continue to look at that list,” he told the judges.

Senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls said they also do not expect to call all of those on the list, citing previous case where he said they “ended up dropping a lot of witnesses for different reasons.”

The final number of prosecution witnesses has yet to be released. But during the case’s first status conference in May, Nicholls said as many 70 witnesses may be presented against the former president during his trial.
These include 31 insider witnesses, 17 crime-base witnesses and 12 witnesses “who are relevant to explain the background and the contextual elements of the crimes charged.”
The prosecutor also intends to call 25 to 30 of these witnesses to give viva voce or verbal testimony during the trial.
Aside from the issue of witnesses, the parties also discussed the defense’s complaints over what it described as a “sheer volume of material” disclosed by the prosecution.
Duterte’s camp is asking the judges to order the prosecution to open a new case file to limit the number of disclosed items to just 10,000.

The trial chamber has yet to issue a written decision on the request, although presiding judge Joanna Korner noted during the hearing that imposing a cap could result in the prosecution violating its disclosure obligations. Duterte’s trial is expected to begin on Nov. 30.

articles.title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
articles.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan had worked for the AI giant for more than a year before he was arrested by the FBI.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters/DOJ
A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)
ByLaura Cress
Technology reporter
A Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".
As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings.
But, here's we do know so far.
Help from a chatbot
The engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).
Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.
Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".
The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.
Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.

The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.
Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.
But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.
Hiding in plain toilet paper
On 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper.
A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.
The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.
When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.
In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".
It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted

blocks.text: Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been inserted
Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan?
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.
Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream.

"These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."

Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt."

On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

articles.title: Pope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery ‘progressing as planned’
articles.summary:
Pontiff has begun walking in his hospital room and is eating normally after operation to remove growth, doctors say

Pope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as…

blocks.text: Pope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as planned, his doctors have said, as the pontiff received good wishes from around the world, including a letter from Britain’s King Charles.

Leo, who had a cancerous mass removed from his right lung late on Tuesday, began walking in his hospital room after respiratory therapy on Wednesday. He was eating normally, his doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria said in a statement issued by the Vatican.
A blood test and chest x-ray showed “normal post-operative progress” and the values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”, they said.

The operation at Rome’s Gemelli hospital confirmed that Leo, 71, has the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has not yet disclosed the results of further tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
The cancer diagnosis for Leo, who was elected the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church in May 2025, has come as a shock.

In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, the pope announced during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup, and that it was “well-contained” and detected early.

Messages have been sent from around the world. King Charles, who is also being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer, would write to Leo privately, a source told Agence France-Presse. Charles and Queen Camilla met the pope when they travelled to the Vatican in October last year.
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, wished Leo a full and swift recovery in a message posted on X, and said the pontiff was “a source of hope and inspiration for billions around the world”.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said he and his wife, Jeanette, were praying for Leo. The couple met the pontiff at the Vatican in May. There has been no reaction yet from Donald Trump, who clashed with Leo earlier this year over the US-Israeli war in Iran, or from the US vice-president, JD Vance, a Catholic.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, wrote on X that Leo’s serenity and strength were an inspiration for all. “We hope for his full and speedy recovery,” she wrote

Before the operation, all of Leo’s appointments until 20 October had been cancelled. He went on a papal trip to France in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.
