articles.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
articles.summary: Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the…

image.caption: The Chinese game 'The Defiant' is set during the Second Sino-Japanese WarImage: 4Divinity

blocks.text: In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

blocks.caption: Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese historyImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.
Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

blocks.caption: 'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular gamesImage: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group

blocks.text: People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.
Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

blocks.caption: The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild"Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse

blocks.text: Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.
No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

blocks.caption: The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and ShanghaiImage: Ubisoft

blocks.text: The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.
Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.
Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

blocks.caption: The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hitImage: Game Science Interactive Technology Co

blocks.text: Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.
The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.
History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."
Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.
This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

articles.title: Police deployment more than doubled to 111,000 for Undas 2026
articles.summary: Over 111,000 policemen will be deployed to enforce security across the country for the observance of All Saints' Day and All Soul's Day on November 1 to 2, more than doubling the manpower compared to…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 7:23pm

Over 111,000 policemen will be deployed to enforce security across the country for the observance of All Saints' Day and All Soul's Day on November 1 to 2, more than doubling the manpower compared to last year.

According to a statement on Wednesday by the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the Philippine National Police (PNP) will beef up security in cemeteries and other areas of convergence.

"The PNP will be deploying 111,582 [police personnel] in 5,628 cemeteries and columbaria," Police Colonel Amante Daro, PNP acting executive officer-Directorate for Operations, said during a DILG forum on Wednesday.
The DILG statement said, "This year's deployment is higher than the police mobilization of over 50,000 cops in last year's Undas."

Of the deployed cops, 11,782 will be personnel from other units. Meanwhile, 31,814 will be force multipliers, including Barangay Peacekeeping Action Teams, PNP advocacy support groups, and local government unit employees who will assist in traffic management.

Aside from cemeteries, there will also be cops stationed at bus terminals and other transportation hubs amid the expected exodus of travelers. Cops will be visible in malls and resorts, the DILG added.
There will also be police patrols in residential communities, the department said.

"May pupunta ng probinsya, iiwanan ang kanilang mga bahay. Minsan buong pamilya wala, so walang tao. Sisiguraduhin ng inyong kapulisan na papatrolyahan 'yon, to make sure na 'di sila mapapasok ng masamang loob, at hindi manakawan ang kanilang tahanan," said Daro.

(Some will go to the province and leave their homes unattended. Sometimes the whole family is away, so no one is left behind. Your police force will ensure that those areas are patrolled to make sure bad elements don't enter and steal from their homes.)

Millions of Filipinos are expected to flock to their home towns and provinces during the annual commemoration to pay respects to their dearly departed loved ones and to reunite with their relatives as well. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine says Musk's SpaceX limits Kyiv's Starlink access
articles.summary: Ukraine accused SpaceX of restricting use of its Starlink system, impacting Kyiv's ability to control its drones as Russian attacks continue unabated.

image.caption: Ukraine depends on Starlink for communications, logistics and drone operationsImage: Andriy Andriyenko/Ukrainian Armed Forces/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office confirmed on Wednesday that the country's military has been cut off from full access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite system as it seeks to defend itself against a now nearly five-year Russian invasion.
Russia launched an unprovoked, illegal, full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.
"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said Presidential Adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov.
"Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.
Starlink cut-off coincides with Trump's 'energy ceasefire'

That political situation refers to US President Donald Trump's recent decision to extend Russian President Vladimir Putin a lifeline by lifting sanctions, buying Russian oil and berating Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — saying he needs to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure and that he should be replaced because "he won't make a deal" with Russia.

Due to rising oil and gas prices brought on by the war in Iran, Trump has repeatedly lashed out at the Ukrainian president, demanding he halt attacks on Russian energy facilities even as Russia continues to target Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure to terrorize the country's citizens as winter approaches.
Trump has insisted, without providing evidence, that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire." But Moscow and Kyiv have both denied this.
On Tuesday evening, for instance, Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv power plant. Ukrainian officials said the Starlink outages had coincided with overnight Russian attacks.
Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia?
SpaceX decision has impacted Ukraine's ability to defend itself
Ukrainian troops use Starlink to conduct drone operations and internet terminals supplied by Elon Musk's company are key to operating long-distance strikes.

Presidential Advisor Beskrestnov said SpaceX had cut off access to its military-grade version of Starlink above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), adding that Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our ‌observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of ‌just 110–120 ​km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," a Reaction Corps representative told Reuters news agency.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said such limitations significantly complicate logistics and ​drone operations.
Ukraine has used Starlink terminals as an alternative to radio control for its drones as well as for ground communications since shortly after Russia launched its invasion.
Starlink's resistance to electronic jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones as well as large hexacopters that drop supplies for Ukraine's frontline troops.
Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a key Donald Trump supporter, has, however, repeatedly shifted his stance on Ukraine since the early days of Russia's invasion.
In August, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Kyiv was looking to create an alternative to Musk's Starlink, in concert "with a European country."

articles.title: Trump's US Super Intelligence Force and AI czar Jay Clayton
articles.summary: Trump announced a new Super Intelligence taskforce with the White House AI czar Jay Clayton in charge of a group responsible for making sure the US leads international competition in artificial…

image.caption: Donald Trump (left) named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton (right) as his AI CzarImage: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the internet" — US President Donald Trump used a comparison borrowed from "many others" to describe artificial intelligence (AI) in his announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force."

The president's move to address the rapid development of the AI industry came after he met with top AI executives at the end of September — and a month before midterm elections in November. Trump has faced intensifying pressure and warnings from business and political leaders about the mostly unregulated technology.

The name echoes Trump's September executive order renaming "Artificial Intelligence" as "Super intelligence" (SI). Jay Clayton, the director of national security and the president's new AI czar, is the task force leader.

The task force will coordinate the government's effort "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," Trump said, and "will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."
How US, China could end the AI race
Trump has made it clear he does not want regulation to "stifle" progress in the SI industry, and a reported charter for the group says it will work to prevent "overregulation and regulatory capture."
What the Super Intelligence Force will do

The White House has not released any information about the Super Intelligence Force, but a copy of a charter detailing the group's responsibilities was reported in The Wall Street Journal and Politico.

The reported document shows the task force's scope is broad, but it names biosecurity and threats to the water supply as areas of focus. Recent cyberattacks have targeted critical infrastructure in the US.
Who is trying to hack the US water supply?

The group is to work with some of the most important US government agencies, including the Pentagon, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), to develop recommendations for new laws to improve government responses.
A legal requirement for AI labs to notify the government of "breaches, hacks and jailbreaks" is to be considered, as well as the potential for automatic alerts.

"Though the labs are ultimately responsible for the risks and opportunities that their models amplify and accelerate, it is the role of the federal government to recognize and understand this era of change and to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced," the reported document says.

The charter's remit includes financial services, energy infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and emergency services. Trump said the task force would coordinate the government's engagement with consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, as well as critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, though some critics noted the omission of workers.

The task force has 120 days to deliver a report on the risks of AI, focusing on potential threats to civil liberties, cybersecurity, standards for advanced models and the impacts of possible overregulation.

blocks.caption: Jay Clayton has been named the chair of Trump's newly announced Super Intelligence Force (SIT)Image: Ken Cedeno/AFP

blocks.text: Who is on the Super Intelligence Force?

Clayton, whom Trump named AI czar in early October, is to chair the task force. He told The Wall Street Journal he expected AI mechanisms to be "developed in dialogue," citing risk models the Securities and Exchange Commission, which he headed during Trump's first presidential term, and the Federal Reserve developed for the financial industry.
The reported charter also named three task force vice chairs:

items: Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the FTC
Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering
Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management

blocks.text: Ferguson is expected to oversee consumer interests and advocacy groups, according to the reported charter. His inclusion comes as the FTC investigates OpenAI, Anthropic and METR over rogue AI agents with potentially nefarious agendas.

Michael, a former tech consultant who sat on Perplexity AI's advisory board, is to oversee coordination with AI companies. Kupor is responsible for coordination with critical infrastructure providers and other industry stakeholders.

Key members of Trump's Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, are also on the task force. The reported charter also listed David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar, and Condoleezza Rice, former secretary of state under President George W. Bush, as external members.

blocks.caption: Former White House AI Czar David Sacks, seen here at the 2024 Republican National Convention, is reportedly an external participant in Trump's new Super Intelligence taskforceImage: Ron Sachs/CNP/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The task force is to report findings and recommendations to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
Response to the task force

According to Politico, several key Republicans were not briefed on plans for the Super Intelligence Force before Trump's announcement. The task force comes as leading Republican Senators prepare major AI legislation intended to mitigate the risks AI poses.

Democrats have criticized the president, with Lori Trahan, a member of the House of Representatives, telling CNN that Trump was "just talking about an AI force without any sort of durable strategy on how to do that through congressional authorization," which felt more like a delay tactic.
"We should be passing legislation and guardrails around the frontier labs. And this doesn't do any of that," Trahan said.
Josh Gottheimer, another Democratic representative, told Politico he was also skeptical of Trump's motives.

"If this is the president waking up, realizing that AI risks aren’t a hoax, and is taking concrete action to protect America, then great," Gottheimer said. "If this is just a PR diversion and an attempt to protect his family’s investments, then I have a massive problem."

articles.title: Rights advocates welcome Duterte appearance at ICC, say victims shouldn't have to wait 'indefinitely'
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte"s second physical appearance at the International Criminal Court (ICC) reinforced victims" rights advocates" call for him to stand trial.

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 6:49pm

THE HAGUE — Former president Rodrigo Duterte’s second physical appearance at the International Criminal Court (ICC) reinforced victims’ rights advocates’ call for him to stand trial, according to Duterte Panagutin Network Europe, whose representatives attended the court’s fourth status conference on Tuesday.

Patricia Enriquez of Duterte Panagutin Network Europe said Duterte’s attendance, alongside the preparation demonstrated by the prosecution and victims’ representatives, was a positive sign as the case moved forward.
“We can see that he is ready to stand trial, which is what we want,” Enriquez said in an interview after the hearing.

She said the prosecution and victims’ representatives appeared organized and prepared with their evidence and documents, adding that cooperation between the prosecution and defense on evidentiary matters was also an important aspect of the proceedings.

“It is very important for people to see that the prosecution and victims’ representatives are ready with their evidence and documents. They are procedurally organized and prepared, and they are also working collaboratively,” she said.

Enriquez said the network and its Dutch counterpart were preparing a campaign week beginning November 27 to welcome supporters traveling from the Philippines and organize activities promoting awareness and support for justice.
Victims’ families in the Philippines were also coming together to empower one another, she added.“Masaya kami na tumutuloy na ang kaso,” Enriquez added.
(We are happy that the trial is proceeding.)

In a statement, the network reiterated that victims and their families should not have to wait indefinitely for justice, criticizing what it described as repeated procedural challenges by Duterte’s defense that threatened to delay proceedings.

“The victims’ families cannot be made to wait indefinitely while the Defense wages procedural battles to delay the proceedings,” the statement said, calling for the case to move forward and for the timely administration of justice to be upheld. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: JV Ejercito flags P206-B realignment in House 2027 budget version
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Finance, on Wednesday questioned the reported realignment of around P206 billion in the House of Representatives" version of the proposed…

blocks.text: Senator JV Ejercito on Wednesday questioned the reported realignment of around P206 billion in the House of Representatives’ version of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.

Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Finance, confirmed that the Senate received the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB) from the House on Tuesday. Copies were distributed to senators and other concerned offices on Wednesday morning, he said.

“Kinukumpirma natin may mga pagbabago, malaking pagbabago mula sa National Expenditure Program at sa House version ng GAB. Ang aking initial reaction, nakakapagtaka lang na tayo’y natanggalan o nabawasan ng pondo sa ilang mga programa,” Ejercito said.

(We confirm that there are significant changes between the National Expenditure Program and the House version of the GAB. My initial reaction is that it is puzzling that funding for certain programs was removed or reduced.)
Among the funding reductions he flagged were:

items: P130 billion for foreign-assisted projects;
P9.5 billion for the calamity fund;
P4.6 billion for flood mitigation structures within major river basins;
P4.4 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program;
P4 billion for the Immunization Program;
P2.6 billion for right-of-way acquisition; and
P2 billion for health promotion.

blocks.text: Ejercito said the transportation sector also suffered a major cut of P40.4 billion, including P19.7 billion intended for the Metro Manila Subway Project (MMSP) and P15 billion for the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR).

The MMSP is a 33-kilometer underground railway designed to provide faster mass transportation across Metro Manila, connecting Valenzuela City to Pasay City, with a spur line to Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3.
The NSCR is a 147-kilometer railway project that will connect Clark in Pampanga to Calamba in Laguna, improving connectivity between Central Luzon, Metro Manila and Southern Luzon.
The Senate finance committee chairperson noted that allocations for some agencies had increased.
The Department of Agriculture (DA), for instance, received a new P10-billion line item for the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk Program.
Ejercito also said the budget for the Department of Health’s Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) Program also increased by P23.9 billion.

For the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), he said the allocation for construction, maintenance, rehabilitation and widening projects increased by P13 billion, while another P8.04 billion was added for flood mitigation structures.

“Ang initial ano ay sa ilang trilyon, almost P206 [billion] ang nagalaw or naiba. So wala na hong naiwan para sa Senado dito na para naman sa mga institutional amendments. Kumbaga limitadong limitado na kami dito,” Ejercito said.

(The initial figure we found was that almost P206 billion had been realigned. So almost nothing was left for the Senate to introduce institutional amendments. In other words, we are extremely limited.)
Nevertheless, Ejercito said the budget process involved balancing competing priorities and that adjustments to budget proposals were normal.

“Ang kailangan lang tiyakin natin na malaman natin ang mga pagbabago, ano ang dahilan at purpose at kung paano mapupunta ba ito sa pangunahing may kailangan. But be reassured that we will always maintain our transparency from the start,” he said.

(We simply need to understand the changes, the reasons and purposes behind them, and how the funds will reach those who need them most. Rest assured that we will maintain transparency from the very beginning.)
He encouraged civil society organizations and watchdog groups to participate in the budget hearings and continue monitoring the process through the bicameral conference committee deliberations.

Ejercito also said he had directed the subcommittees of the Senate Committee on Finance to submit their reports by Friday, October 23, ahead of the start of plenary budget deliberations on November 23.
On Monday, the House of Representatives approved its version of the GAB on third and final reading, with 281 votes in favor, 13 against and one abstention.

Lawmakers who voted against the measure, including Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno, due to the cuts in the budget allocations for education and public services, and increased allocations for patronage-driven assistance.
He also decried the lack of transparency and meaningful participation in the budget process.

"The budget is a reflection of our values. We cannot tell our people that we have no money for their children’s schools and their families’ medicine, while finding hundreds of billions for unvetted infrastructure and political discretion,” Diokno said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Trump heads to rallies in Arizona and Montana after campaign stop-off in Alaska – US politics live
articles.summary:
Trump has taken to campaigning in conservative-leaning ​parts of competitive states, rather than in more politically diverse areas

The family of a British man who was killed by a…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 6m agoFamily of man killed by tiger criticise online content as Trump mocks fatal incident
26m agoTrump heads to Arizona and Montana after campaign stop-off in conservative Alaska

blocks.text: Family of man killed by tiger criticise online content as Trump mocks fatal incident
The family of a British man who was killed by a tiger at a wildlife park have spoken of their “severe distress” after Donald Trump shared a video of the incident on social media.
The president posted footage of William Chapman, 23, being fatally attacked by a tiger at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park to 13m followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday evening.
Trump accompanied the short clip – which showed the animal biting and clawing Chapman as he sat in the enclosure, but not him being killed – with the signed message: “Don’t ever mess with nature!”
On Wednesday morning Trump followed this up with another post – this time an AI-generated video of him grappling with a tiger, which appears to mimic the original.
The clip, which is accompanied by the song ‘The Lion Sleeps Tonight’, features the president copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him hugging the animal.
Chapman’s family said in a statement that “deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress”.

They also posted a tribute describing him as a “bright, warm and engaging young man” and questioning what part his “significant mental illness over a number of years” and prescribed strong medication played in the incident.
Trump heads to Arizona and Montana after campaign stop-off in conservative Alaska
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump will attend campaign rallies in Arizona and Montana later today, having spent the past 24 hours in Alaska – a sign of his party’s recent polling woes.
Conservative Alaska is one of several where the Democrats have a chance of flipping a Senate seat amid voter dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the Iran war.
Polling has shown Democratic candidate Mary Peltola tied ⁠or slightly ahead of incumbent Republican senator Dan ⁠Sullivan in a state the president carried by 14 percentage points in 2024.

Here, as in much of the United States, the president’s approval rating is flopping, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices and a conflict in the Middle East that has proven deeply unpopular with voters.

Opening for Trump, Sullivan acknowledged that Alaskans face “challenges” when it comes to energy costs. But “the conflict in the Middle East is temporary,” he said. “The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas ⁠and our jobs.“
The president has taken to campaigning in conservative-leaning ​parts of competitive states, rather than in more politically diverse areas with more votes potentially up for grabs.
At one point, Trump pardoned two local repair shop owners who were convicted of violating the federal Clean Air Act for removing pollution controls on diesel engines.
He also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail – a process he has repeatedly sought to curtail and discredit. Trump will spend Wednesday campaigning in Arizona and Montana.
In other developments:

items: In Alaska, Donald Trump repeated his false claim that he had to start his war on Iran because, “they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. In fact, US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003. Despite that assessment, in the summer of 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment facilities which he later claimed had “obliterated” the country’s nuclear program. Eight months after that, he launched a full-scale war on Iran justified, he now says, by Iran being just weeks away from getting the bomb.

Aboard Air Force One on his way to Alaska for a campaign rally, the president of the United States posted video of a British man who was fatally mauled by a tiger last week on his social media platform with the mocking caption: “Don’t ever mess with nature!”

The new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, passed on an opportunity to set the record straight on whether she is licensed to practice law anywhere in the United States. Asked “Where did you pass the bar exam?” Zacharia just said: “I moved to China.”

articles.title: CICC warns of online grooming tactics, from love-bombing to blackmail
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Wednesday warned that online grooming involves several stages of manipulation, including isolation, love-bombing and blackmail, which…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 6:03pm

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Wednesday warned that online grooming involves several stages of manipulation, including isolation, love-bombing and blackmail, which could lead to violence or suicide among young victims.

Speaking at the Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon public briefing, CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato Paraiso said nihilistic violent extremism (NVE), which authorities suspect may have contributed to a series of school shootings, involves different levels of manipulation that could lead to various outcomes.

Paraiso said online groomers typically target children through gaming and social media platforms, where they assess their potential victims' interests, including their attitudes toward violence and sexual content, before befriending them.
“After that, they move [victims] to messaging platforms such as Discord and Telegram, which are more private. There are also communities within these platforms,” Paraiso said.
He said groomers then attempt to gain their victims' trust and emotional dependence through a tactic known as love-bombing.
“In those communities, they make [victims] feel loved through what we call love-bombing. The goal is for the group to replace the family structure,” he added.
NVE refers to an extremist mindset that embraces violence, destruction or mass harm without necessarily pursuing a conventional political, religious or ideological goal.

Unlike traditional extremist movements, which often seek to advance a defined cause or worldview, NVE may be driven by nihilism, alienation, a desire for notoriety or an online community's glorification of violence.
According to Paraiso, groomers initially ask victims to perform seemingly harmless tasks, such as taking selfies, while offering praise and encouragement to gain their trust.
The demands gradually escalate to more serious and potentially incriminating acts, including committing crimes or sending nude photographs.
Paraiso said groomers could then use these materials to blackmail victims, threatening to release the images or expose their actions if they tell their families about the abuse.
He warned that the final stage of manipulation could lead to extreme violence or suicide, although not all cases result in school shootings.
“In the final stage, victims may either carry out school shootings or, more commonly, although we do not always see it, young people take their own lives,” Paraiso said.
The warning comes amid concerns over three school shooting incidents reported in the Philippines in 2026.
In June, three students were killed when two suspects opened fire on their classmates at a public high school in Tacloban City.
In August, a student shot a schoolmate before turning the gun on himself in Zamboanga.
A similar incident occurred in South Cotabato in September, when a student shot a schoolmate before taking his own life.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Trump announces plans for major oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland
articles.summary: The US president has claimed Greenland holds vast and easily accessible oil reserves without providing evidence or details. His announcement follows a deal expanding the US military presence on the…

image.caption: Greenland's vast natural resources have attracted growing US interest, with President Donald Trump announcing plans for major oil, gas and mineral exploration (FILE 19/07/2008)Image: Ashley Cooper/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said major oil, gas and mineral exploration was set to begin in Greenland.
His announcement follows a security agreement between the United States, Denmark and the Arctic island's leaders.
What has Trump said about Greenland's resources?
Trump offered no details about which companies would be involved, where exploration would take place or when operations would begin.
"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He also claimed that experts believed Greenland held some of the world's largest deposits of easily accessible oil, without providing evidence.

Greenland is believed to hold substantial untapped oil reserves, but their commercial viability remains uncertain due to high extraction costs, harsh Arctic conditions and environmental restrictions. No commercial oil production has been established in Greenland.
Greenland has significant mineral resources, including rare earth elements used in electronics, renewable energy technologies and military equipment.
What's really in the Greenland deal?
The island has also attracted interest for its potential oil and gas reserves, although exploration in the harsh Arctic environment presents considerable technical and economic challenges.
In August, reports that a US oil company was preparing operations in a remote part of eastern Greenland prompted unease among residents and local authorities.
Trump did not say whether his announcement was connected to those activities.
Why is Greenland strategically important to the US?
In the same post, Trump described Greenland's strategic location as "second to none" for US and European security.
"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland," he claimed, adding that US defenses there would be able to intercept missiles, drones and other weapons.
Greenland lies along one of the shortest routes between Russia and North America, making it strategically important for missile detection and defense.
Its location is also significant for Trump's proposed "Golden Dome" missile defense system.
Melting Arctic ice has meanwhile increased interest in potential new shipping routes through the region.
What does the US security deal with Greenland involve?
In September, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement aimed at easing tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the island, including by force.
Under the 10-page agreement, Washington will establish two additional military bases, at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in the east.
The US already operates the Pituffik Space Base in northern Greenland.

The agreement expands the American military presence and provides for cooperation on missile defense, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination.
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Trump's earlier demands for US control of the island had strained relations between Washington and Copenhagen, both NATO allies.

articles.title: SC: Senior citizen discounts can't be combined with other discounts
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that discounts for senior citizens cannot be combined with other discounts, thus these price reductions cannot be applied on top of other promotions or discounts…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 5:32pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that discounts for senior citizens cannot be combined with other discounts, thus these price reductions cannot be applied on top of other promotions or discounts provided by businesses.

In a press briefer, the SC said that when goods or services are offered at promotional prices, senior citizens may choose either the promotional discount or the 20% senior citizen discount, whichever gives them greater savings.
"Granting an additional discount beyond what the law allows would unfairly benefit the customer at the business expense," the SC said.

The ruling stemmed from a case filed against a general manager of a hotel in Bacolod City for alleged violation of Republic Act 7432 or the Senior Citizens Act. The hotel executive was acquitted in the ruling.

Under the law, as amended by the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, Filipinos aged 60 and above are entitled to benefits and privileges, including a 20% discount on services in hotels, restaurants, and recreation centers.
According to the SC, the general manager was charged for refusing to grant two senior citizens their discounts.
However, the general manager argued that the hotel had already applied the 20% discount on the room rate negotiated by a club that the senior citizens were members.
The Municipal Trial Court in Cities, Regional Trial Court, and Court of Appeals found the general manager guilty.
For its part, the SC reversed the rulings, saying the hotel was not required to grant an additional 20% discount.
It said that while the Senior Citizens Act aims to protect and support senior citizens, its implementation must also be fair to businesses.

"[T]he State's pursuit of public welfare cannot be allowed to impose undue or confiscatory burdens on private establishments, whose continued viability is essential to the long-term effectiveness of the law," it said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: El Niño may affect small pelagic fish catch, says fishers group
articles.summary: The potentially strong El Niño may affect fishing activities, including the catch of small pelagic fishes, a fishers group said on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 5:24pm
The potentially strong El Niño may affect fishing activities, including the catch of small pelagic fishes, a fishers group said on Wednesday.

“Basically, it is possible that the fishing catch will change. But for now, it is still in normal conditions,” said Association of Fresh Fish Traders of the Philippines president Jonjon Santos in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB in Filipino.
“The most affected will be the small pelagics, such as the galunggong (round scad), sardines. They are very sensitive to temperatures, the so-called water column,” he added.
El Niño occurs when sea surface temperature rises, according to PAGASA.
The state weather bureau earlier said that average temperature across the Philippines is set to rise by 1 to 2 degrees Celsius during the weather phenomenon.
Citing the 1983 strong El Niño, the group said that fish production dropped significantly after a year.
“So it means that for small fish, the water column or thermocline can be strong,” said Santos.
The group said that it has yet to monitor any cases of unwarranted price increase in fish products as it is closed fishing season.
“When November comes, until February, you know, we are in closed fishing season. So there is no production,” said Santos. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Fact check: Misleading graph about alleged Russian bot activity
articles.summary: Did attacks on Russian data centers reduce bot activity around Germany's AfD? A viral graph claims they did. But it contains significant inconsistencies and provides no evidence to support the claim.

image.caption: The graph shows significant inconsistencies, and its data source is unclearImage: x.com/tomaszdechovsky

blocks.text: After Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers operated by the Russian technology company Yandex, claims began circulating online that the strikes had disrupted or even halted the activity of Russian propaganda bots. These accounts are often accused of spreading disinformation or artificially amplifying content on social media.

During the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also suggested that the attacks on Yandex data centers had disrupted bot activity, saying "there was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations [because] there were fewer bots." In response to BBC Verify, Zelenskyy's office said that, rather than referring to reduced bot activity, the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media." The office added that it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.

So far, however, there is no clear evidence linking the attacks to a decline in bot activity. According to Josef Holnburger, managing director of the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), there is currently "no decline in Russian disinformation activities that could be explained by the attack on Yandex data centers." CeMAS systematically monitors such campaigns.
European lawmaker shares graph without evidence on X

Nevertheless, a misleading graph has been circulated as supposed evidence. It was shared, for example, by Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský. His post was viewed more than four million times on X. He suggested that the graph might demonstrate a decline in "online activity around AfD," although he did not specify what kind of activity he meant. In reality, the graph most likely demonstrates nothing at all.

blocks.caption: A Czech Member of the European Parliament linked the graph to an alleged decline in online activity surrounding the AfDImage: x.com/tomaszdechovsky

blocks.text: The German-language graph is titled "Daily activity over 3 months." It appears to show activity remaining relatively stable before dropping sharply in early October, roughly coinciding with the attacks on Yandex data centers. However, nothing in the graph itself indicates that this relates to AfD-related online activity.
No source and faulty scaling

The same applies to the graph's underlying data. It is unclear which data were used. No source is provided, nor is there any explanation of the data collection process or calculation method for the alleged "activity," which initially ranges between 6,000 and 7,000 before falling below 3,000.

Particularly striking is that the graph extends to October 15. Its final data point appears to correspond to October 14 – a date that was still in the future when the graph first appeared online on October 11. Data for a future date cannot exist.

The graph also contains scaling errors on both the X and Y axes. For example, on the Y axis, the distance between 2,500 and 3,000 is smaller than the other 500-unit intervals. Because the Y axis does not begin at zero, the decline is visually exaggerated. On the X axis, equal periods of time are represented by unequal distances.

It is also unclear which platforms were analyzed and how the variable "activity" was calculated. The absence of a known data source, the inaccurate scaling, and the inclusion of "future" values strongly suggest that this is not a meaningful graph based on factual data and sound statistical methods.
AI involvement cannot be proven, but is possible
It is unclear whether AI was used to create the graph. Given the errors and the apparent "hallucination" of presenting future data, AI involvement cannot be ruled out.

Misleading and error-filled graphs, some of which may have been AI-generated, appear regularly. German public broadcaster BR's #Faktenfuchs team recently reported on one such graph that falsely depicted industrial production in Germany (article in German). False or fabricated graphs can lend credibility to unsupported claims.
The identity of the graph's creator remains unknown.
What do Cloudflare data actually show?

Cloudflare data are also frequently cited in connection with claims of declining bot activity. However, according to CeMAS managing director Holnburger, there is a misunderstanding about what Cloudflare's report actually means. Cloudflare provides services to many websites that block traffic assessed as non-human. Automated web traffic is common and includes, for example, crawlers that check websites for freshly published content. Search engines, including Yandex, rely on these crawlers. Other bots may be used for spam in comment sections.
In a message to #Faktenfuchs Holnburger writes, "a decline in bot activity on websites is something entirely different from a decline in inauthentic behavior by social bots on social networks."

Referring to Cloudflare data, he added: "When looking at overall activity from Russian IP addresses on servers using Cloudflare services, there is no major decline in bot activity." Furthermore, there is no reason to assume that the infrastructure used by disinformation-related social bots would be hosted on Yandex data centers. "It is more likely that these systems are distributed across many different providers," Holnburger writes.
The article was originally written in German and adapted into English by Alima de Graaf

articles.title: Do non-German nationals commit more crimes than Germans?
articles.summary: People without German passports appear more frequently in German police crime statistics than German nationals. A new study explains why.

image.caption: There are many factors contributing to crime, as a recent data analysis showsImage: Boris Roessler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Every year, when the Federal Criminal Police Office publishes the police crime statistics, theAlternative for Germany (AfD) — a party that is, in part, right-wing extremist — pays particularly close attention. They are looking for crimes committed by refugees, migrants and foreigners living in Germany. But studies by media scholars show that 95% of the AfD's press releases focus on non-German suspects, while crimes involving German suspects are almost completely ignored.
However, the common narrative of the AfD — that non-Germans are inherently much more violent — is simply not true.

In a new research paper, Susann Prätor, a sociologist, criminologist and professor at the Lower Saxony Police Academy, has taken a very close look at crime data in Germany, together with her colleagues from the University of Zurich and the Lower Saxony Criminological Research Institute. She looked not only at officially reported crime — that is, all offenses that appeared in police crime statistics — but also at unreported crime: these are all offenses that are not reported or detected, and therefore do not appear in any official statistics but are identified through representative surveys.

Prätor told DW: "Yes, according to police crime statistics, people who do not have German citizenship commit crimes more frequently than German citizens. However, studies into unreported cases show that non-German nationals are twice as likely to be reported. Differences between the two groups are also evident in crimes that go unreported, but they are significantly less pronounced."
German offenders are reported to the police much less frequently
Crimes committed by foreign nationals are therefore twice as likely to appear in police crime statistics as crimes committed by Germans.
These statistics record all reported cases and do not specify whether the allegations prove to be true.

When the statistics are adjusted for the bias in the reporting of crimes, foreigners are no longer 2.6 times more likely to commit crimes than Germans, but only 1.7 times more likely. This figure is also consistent with the results of studies on unreported juvenile violent crime. According to these studies, foreign youths are about 1.6 times as likely to commit violent crimes as German youths.

Other factors affecting crime include age and gender. Young men make up a larger proportion of the foreign-born population, and young men are the group most prone to criminal behavior across all societies.

According to Prätor, "Categories such as being young, male, poorly educated and having a history of violence are factors that increase the likelihood of violent behavior. A certain concept of masculinity also plays a role, wherever that may come from. But we do not see culture as a factor, contrary to the prejudice that masculinity and violence play a greater role in other cultures."
Prätor points to a survey on attitudes toward violence. According to the survey, 5% of German youths view violence positively. Among those without a German passport, the figure is 10%.

The criminologist has identified a crucial factor: "Family upbringing plays an important role in shaping attitudes toward violence, because these attitudes are formed in the home. If I experience violence in my own home, I will have a different relationship to violence than if I hadn't experienced it," said Prätor.

Germany is, however, on the right track, says Prätor, even if it doesn't always feel that way. "Fifty or sixty years ago, parental violence was much more common in child-rearing than it is today. Acts of violence committed by young people are also far less frequent than they were in the 1990s or the early 2000s."

Susann Prätor emphasizes that it is important to bring objectivity to the debate. A good illustration of this is a look at police records of serious violent crimes — such as aggravated assault, manslaughter, or murder. "Of every 100 German citizens, 0.2% commit violent crimes; among non-German nationals, the figure is 0.6%."

However, Prätor points out, "More than 99% of the people living here in Germany — whether of German or non-German origin — the overwhelming majority in this country do not commit any serious violent crimes at all."
Survivors: Timeline to punish rape in Germany is too short
Germany must do more to prevent crime

Prätor also trains prospective police officers. She wants to send the message to policymakers that they should place greater emphasis on the positive aspects of migration. She argues that the debate on immigration is far too negative, largely due to an overly narrow focus on police crime statistics. The vast majority of non-Germans integrate exceptionally well, she says.

She wants the government to invest more money in prevention: "By starting as early as possible with children and adolescents: strengthening social skills as early as preschool, building on that in school and responding when incidents of violence do occur. It's also important to invest in infrastructure and recreational activities in certain regions. After all, a key factor in youth violence — regardless of background — is that young people lack a meaningful daily structure."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Joni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’
articles.summary:
Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram

Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The…

blocks.text: Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”
It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.
At a concert in 2024, Mitchell said: “Fuck Donald Trump, I love that song,” referring to the rap track by YG. She added: “I wish I could vote ... I’m a Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”

Mitchell was born in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in 1943, and eventually settled with her family in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Her earliest gigs were at folk clubs there, followed by Calgary and Toronto, where she met US folk singer Chuck Mitchell. They married in 1965 and Mitchell moved to the US. The marriage didn’t last, ending two years later, but by that time Mitchell had established herself as a mellifluous, original voice on the vibrant US folk music circuit.

blocks.caption: Folk original … Joni Mitchell in 1968. Photograph: Jack Robinson/Getty Images

blocks.text: She released her debut album in 1968, and soon after, using the album’s royalties, moved to Los Angeles’ Laurel Canyon where she recorded her first gold-selling album, Ladies of the Canyon. She remained based in California and currently lives in Santa Barbara.

Mitchell’s most recent studio album is Shine, from 2007. After that she spent a number of years out of the public eye, suffering a brain aneurysm in 2015 that required extensive recovery. But she returned to live performance in 2022 with an unannounced set at the Newport folk festival, and has since performed a number of all-star “Joni Jam” concerts.

A biopic about her is being prepared by director Cameron Crowe, who began work on it in the early 2020s. Earlier this year, record executive Clive Davis announced at a party that Meryl Streep would play Mitchell in the film.

articles.title: FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football
articles.summary: Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and history at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for greater structure globally.

image.caption: North Korea have one of the best youth teams in women's football in the world, but questions are being asked about baseline support for women in the gameImage: IPA Sport/ABACA/IMAGO

blocks.text: At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first on the continent, will be the last with 32 teams but is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is a moment of history as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.
Women's game falling short on global standards

But even the handful of players who makes it from these youth tournaments to a professional career, making a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.
The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The average club contract length is 1.6 years.

"If you know the global average is $2,600, but then the median drops by $1,000 to just over $1,600 so that that gives you an indication of the kind of the salary range that that we're dealing with here," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"I think what you also find in the in the women's game is the the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," said Brown. "In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and and not being paid paid at all."
With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement. "Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures – including extra workload and social media abuse - but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich are one of the biggest clubs in the world, but Germany also has gaps when it comes to baseline support for women playing professional footballImage: O. Behrendt/Contrast/IMAGO

blocks.text: Germany aiming to be example of development

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier - in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year - the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German FA (DFB) rule reveals that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.
Ultimately, the faster the game grows the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

articles.title: Ukrainian soldiers in combat have access to Starlink satellite internet restricted
articles.summary:
Outage of terminals managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX comes as Russia launches ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from US

Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had…

blocks.text: Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.

The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the high-speed terminals on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.

Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Musk, an ally of Trump, had previously cut off Starlink service to Ukrainian soldiers during an offensive that took a small amount of Russian territory.

Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
after newsletter promotion

Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.

Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit several power plants and key substations that carry electricity to the capital, including from a major power plant.

“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” he said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.

articles.title: The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech
articles.summary: Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smart watches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of…

image.caption: Cheap mini fans used for a month in summer are often end up forgotten at the bottom of a drawer or in the trash Image: Luis Soto/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.
"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

blocks.caption: Cheap e-vapes are part of the rising trend of fast tech that is adding to the growing e-waste crisis Image: Joel Carrett/AAP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.
This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.
The Great Wall of e-waste and what to do about it

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.
In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.
Recycling rare earths in Germany to reduce China dependence
In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.
These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.
"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she told DW.
Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.
But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.
Healthcare's increasing digital waste problem
Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors, and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

blocks.caption: Even small, cheap electronics should be recycled as they contain valuable materials Image: Desmond Tiro/DW

blocks.text: A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.
That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.
"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.
How wearables are revolutionizing heart health

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."
A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

blocks.caption: Many digital health devices could be reused or recycled if designed properly Image: Marko Prpic/PIXSELL/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Green nudges' help citizens to recycle

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges"such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person, motivate people to "do the right thing."

articles.title: Leaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed for violating ban on protest site
articles.summary:
Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authorities

Two leaders of India’s…

blocks.text: Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.

A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.

CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.

“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.

On Saturday, the CJP – a movement with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.

The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.

blocks.caption: Delhi police inspect vehicles near the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi on Tuesday. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The election commission has ​denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters ‌can re-enrol.

Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained.

In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar, provoking outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das ‌were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.

The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it an “unwarranted and constitute an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
It was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed reporting
